speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: Not very long ago there was constituted by this house a special committee on estimates. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the facts of the rye transaction are not as stated, in the newspapers. During the current year we have a quota into the United States of 50433-355
Inquiries of the Ministry
3,300,000	bushels of rye. A reference was made recently to the tariff commission having to do with the continuance of that quota. After hearing witnesses the tariff commission recommended to the president that the quota be reduced 50 per cent to 1,650,000 bushels. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe, Port Arthur (for Mr. St. Laurent) for the second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Brooks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think one of the most extraordinary and one of the most unbelievable aspects of this whole controversy is the fact that the Prime Minister, who sponsored this bill, has refused to stand up in this house and defend it against the very severe criticism which it has received from the opposition and from the press right across Canada, irrespective of what party they normally support.
I think that the Prime Minister, by refusing to take part in this debate, is showing contempt both for parliament and for the press of this country. On Tuesday the Minister of Defence Production tried to excuse the Prime Minister's absence from this debate by saying that he spoke only on important bills. Now, surely the Prime Minister does not consider a bill which undermines provincial jurisdiction over property and civil rights is an unimportant bill. I certainly hope he will rise in his place very soon and defend this very bad bill against the criticism which has so justifiably been directed against it.
As a matter of fact, I think the Prime Minister, like the majority of the cabinet and the other Liberal members of the house, has no real liking for this bill. I think they all realize that if these wide and all-inclusive powers, which make the Minister of Defence Production a virtual dictator over industry, both in peacetime and in war, are granted, then this bill when it becomes an act will prove to be a very serious political liability to the Liberal party at the next election. I think they realize that. That I think is the reason why the Prime Minister does not speak. He has no heart for this bill. He does not support it. I think he has been forced into it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Why do you oppose it, then?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
If the majority of the Liberal party and the cabinet are, as it is very reliably believed here, against this bill, why is it being pushed forward? I have done a lot of thinking about this and have talked to a lot of people. The conclusion I come to is that the reason why the bill is being pushed forward by the minister is that he 50433-355i
Defence Production Act is smarting under the defeat he received this spring in the cabinet over the pipe-line issue. It is very reliably reported around parliament hill that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to back down from his original project of an all-Canadian pipe line, and has been forced by his colleagues to accept an alternative, which is a gas exchange policy with the United States.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would speak to the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Where is the relevancy there?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The story widely circulated on parliament hill is that the Minister of Defence Production has said that either the cabinet will back him on this measure, or he will resign. I do not think they are ready to have him resign at the present time. And so we see the government going forward with a bill which the Winnipeg Free Press very rightly describes as imprecise, illiberal, feeble, lamentably bad, and as the lazy, playing-safe alternative beloved of bureaucracy. That same paper goes on to advise the government that as it has become jammed into a position which is as painful as it is undignified, it should drop this bill. I think that is some of the best advice that has been given for some time by a serious-minded supporter of this government.
This bill has been described by the Liberal press as bad in principle; and as the Winnipeg Free Press has so well put it, it is bad in principle because the circumstances are fundamentally different today from what they were in 1951, when this bill was first introduced. The Free Press says that for the minister to argue that there is an emergency today is simply ludicrous. Referring to that particular statement, I should like to go back to the debate of last Tuesday and quote an interchange that took place as reported at page 5380 of Hansard. The Minister of Defence Production is there quoted as saying this:
They say,-
"They" is referring to the opposition.
-"Yes, but the atomic bomb threat is not very serious-"

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Nonsense! Nobody said that in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: My hon. friend was absent from the house this morning-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Nobody said that in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It was said this morning in this house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Give the quotation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I shall certainly give it if I can get the blue sheets.
The minister has now had plenty of time to get the blue sheets and to go through Hansard. I should like to ask him what is the line and page in Hansard where an
5624	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act opposition member is reported to have made the statement which he contended had been made.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You said it was ludicrous, which is the same thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am asking the minister it he will tell me where to find that statement which he has said positively was made in this house on Tuesday morning last. I should like him to tell me when it was said and by whom. He said he would be glad to see who had said it and to give the line and quotation when he had received the blue sheets. He has had several days in which to get hold of the blue sheets and to read Hansard. I have gone through Hansard and have studied it carefully; and as far as I can see, that statement was not made. I ask the minister to tell me who made the statement and where we can find it in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am sorry but my time has been fully occupied on a salmon river.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: On what?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Salmon fishing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You will note, Mr. Speaker, that according to the minister fishing salmon is much more important than is the matter of dealing with a bill of this magnitude.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The minister said it himself. So, Mr. Speaker, you can see why the Winnipeg Free Press says that statements made by the minister are ludicrous. I say it is just an example of the kind of statements which we have been getting from the minister, and which make you wonder just how much credence you can give to any statement made on important matters of this kind.
As the Free Press again has said, the bringing in of this bill can only be explained by the lack of foresight which has been shown by the minister's colleagues in allowing the bill to come forward. It finally concludes these very objective comments on this whole matter by saying that the government's persistence in pushing this bill forward will leave a nasty taste in the mouth of all Liberal members who, through their respect for the minister and through their faithfulness to him, will rise in the house and vote for it. It further goes on to say that the opposition will not need to exaggerate to make the government appear weak, foolish tMr. Hees.]

and bureaucratic, because it says that is what the government is being if it sticks to this bill. That is a clear, objective criticism of the government's whole attitude in this matter by one of the great newspapers of this country. I think that the minister and the government would do well to consider carefully the criticism which has been levelled against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware of the fact that the same great newspaper has published a more recent editorial?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The hon. member had better get his reading up to date.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I should just like the minister to answer this editorial. Let us just take it editorial by editorial and clear the matter up as we go along.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Why do you not keep up to date for a change?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I would say that this is fairly up to date. The minister last Tuesday, as reported at page 5378 of Hansard, said:
Other provisions of the act affect property, but there is no provision in the Defence Production Act that affects the freedom of any person.
Following that statement I should like to refer the minister to section 31 of the Defence Production Act, subsection 2, paragraph (d). First of all, section 1 reads as follows:
31. (1) The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he deems necessary to control and regulate the production, processing, distribution, acquisition, disposition or use of essential materials or the supply or use of essential services for the purposes of
(a)	ensuring the availability of defence supplies or the construction or operation of defence projects for the defence requirements of Canada and for co-operative arrangements for defence being carried on by Canada and associated governments* or
(b)	ensuring that abnormal requirements of essential materials and services for defence supplies or defence projects are obtained in the manner least likely to cause disruption of the trade and commerce of Canada dependent on those materials and services, which disruption might impede or prejudice the defence preparations or the economic stability of Canada.
Then subsection 2 reads as follows:
(2) Subject to the regulations, if any, the minister may, by order, as he deems necessary for the purposes specified in subsection (1), . . .
and paragraph (d) reads as follows:
(d) require any person who supplies any essential service to supply the service to such persons, to such extent and on such conditions as the minister may prescribe;
Mr. Speaker, as I read that section, it gives the minister complete jurisdiction over hours and conditions of work of those who work in what the minister, in his discretion, may describe as an essential defence industry in

peacetime; and if those working in an industry which the minister, in his discretion, designates as a defence industry disagree with the extent-which is the hours of work-or the conditions of work which the minister may prescribe, then it appears to me that this act denies to those workers the right to strike in protest during peacetime.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: That is a section which we will under no circumstances accept, a section which denies in peacetime to those working in an industry which the minister may designate as a defence industry the right to take the only kind of effective action which is afforded to labour to protest-namely by the formal strike-in peacetime against conditions of work and hours of labour which the minister in his wisdom may prescribe.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: That is a legal opinion that is very unsound indeed, in my opinion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It shows great erudition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Will you abolish the labour unions too?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Further, in section 28, the minister assumes the right to cancel any contract. Section 28, subsection 1, of the act reads as follows:
The governor in council may, by order, direct that a person shall not be bound by any obligation, restriction or limitation imposed on that person by or under any statute, order, rule, regulation, bylaw or contract with respect to such matters as may be specified in the order affecting the entry into or performance of a defence contract by that person or the carrying out of an order made by the minister under this act.
That simply gives the minister the right during peacetime to cancel any labour contract. These are the kind of things, Mr. Speaker, for which we do not believe there is any justification in peacetime. Under these sections the minister simply assumes the right to cancel a labour contract and to designate the hours of work or conditions under which working people shall work in an industry which he designates as a defence industry. That gives him complete and dictatorial power over all of industry, because all the minister has to do at any time to assume these powers is to designate, in his wisdom or lack of it, that a certain industry is a defence industry.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the kind of thing for which we will not stand. We believe that the right of labour to protest, in the only way it has at its disposal, against hours of work and conditions of work, namely, the right to strike in peacetime, must be preserved, and we do not intend to see this
Defence Production Act minister or any other minister or this government take away from labour-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You know this bill does not do that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: -the right to strike in peacetime. That is exactly what these sections say, and the minister has not denied what I have said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It has been denied.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I now deny it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The minister simply gets up and says that he denies it-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: We do not want to be as foolish as the present speaker.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: -exactly as he got up and said, as found at page 5380 of Hansard of June 28, that we had said that the atomic bomb threat is not very serious.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You said it was ludicrous a minute ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: No member of the opposition ever said anything like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You just said it was ludicrous a moment ago.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: So when the minister gets up and makes the positive statement that a certain thing is or is not so, how can we believe his statement in view of what he said on that occasion which has been proved to be untrue? I believe it gives us cause to think many times about the validity of statements made by the minister. I see that the minister's answer to statements he cannot answer is simply to get up and walk out of the house. That is an example of the attitude of the minister. It is obvious that the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) throughout this whole debate is that he simply does not believe in the bill. If the minister sponsoring a bill should not speak on it, who in the world should? Of course the Prime Minister should speak on the bill. Otherwise, why did he sponsor it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Repetition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
He is not speaking simply because his heart is not in it. He agrees with the majority of his colleagues in the cabinet that the bill should never have been brought forward. Defence Production Act stand up when the votes are called and do what they are told, as they so often do. This shows what a lamentable state a government can get into if it has been in office too long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production

speechtext:
As found at page 5382 of Hansard of June 28, the minister said:
The situation has reached the point where the government must insist that this legislation be passed.
In other words, we have come to the time when the government is not even going to make the pretence of listening to the arguments of the opposition. With its big majority in the house it is going to demand that this measure be jammed through. There is dictatorship if I ever saw dictatorship.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You have never seen it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: It shows that when a government is in power too long it forgets about parliament and the people. It simply decides it is going to have its own way, and that is all. This dictatorship is being imposed on parliament and the country in peacetime, denying labour the right to strike, denying the sanctity of labour contracts-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You do not like it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: -but in any event the particular point on which I wanted to rise is that the hon. member apparently is under the impression that we are in committee. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
What about you and all the

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext: He does not indulge in anything else.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I protest.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext: Yes, it has, Mr. Speaker. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
If the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) wishes to appeal this ruling I shall be very pleased to give him the opportunity. However, I just want to point out to him standing order No. 41 which reads:
No member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, nor of any of the royal family; nor of the governor or person administering the government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof.
Who is going to say whether or not the words are offensive, the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) or the Speaker? It just so happens it is my duty to interpret those expressions. I let one go by, and in so far as this one was concerned, I thought that in order to make sure we did not have derisive expressions against hon. members appearing in our records, I would ask the reporter to strike it off the record. Now, when I do that, I do it as a matter of order. There

Defence Production Act are other examples in our practice of expressions being stricken from the record of this house. Mr. Speaker Lemieux did it; Mr. Speaker Black did it on several occasions, as did Mr. Speaker Casgrain. I have done it myself on at least two or three occasions since I became Speaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
May I say a word, Mr. Speaker. I recognize the correctness of what Your Honour has said to the effect that previous Speakers, like yourself, have on occasions expunged certain references from Hansard. I hope Your Honour will permit me to take just a moment to express strong objection to that practice, except on very rare occasions. I am not at this moment discussing whether or not the words used by the hon. member for Broadview were offensive. I will say parenthetically that I think they were intended to suggest disrespect for a member of the house. I do not believe we should treat each other that way. The words were not naughty words which people could not read and still maintain their morals. However, they are not the kind of words that gentlemen should use about each other, in view of the fact we are sitting here as the representatives of the people of Canada.
Having said that, it seems to me that expunging remarks from Hansard should take place on only rare occasions. In fact, I feel it should take place only when remarks have been used containing the kind of words which, in themselves, should not appear on the record of parliament. As a matter of fact, if the hon. member for Broadview has indulged in the use of disrespectful words he should not have the privilege of having those words stricken from Hansard. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have not taken part in the debate since the resolution was introduced in March. I listened to the minister when he spoke in the house on Tuesday, June 28, and over the week end I had an opportunity to read some of the speeches that were made in the earlier stages by both the minister and the leader of this group. It is largely as a result of some of the statements that have been made that I feel inclined to speak at this time in order to try to clarify some of the issues.
I was interested in the minister's statement at page 5377 of Hansard when he said:
We have seen many legitimate objections to the bill drowned in a torrent of exaggeration, and the corpses of the arguments are now floating around in a vast ocean of words.
If at this stage anyone knows what the argument against the bill is I am sure that I cannot be one of that number.
I agree with the minister that, after reading these speeches, there is a vast ocean of words. But may I draw attention to these words:
We have seen many legitimate objections-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: May I correct something there? It should read "any". It was a misprint. I did not make that correction in Hansard. I intended to say "any", and I think I did say "any", although I have noticed in reading Hansard that the letter "m" is in, but it should not be in. I meant to use the word "any".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The minister will admit that there may be some legitimate objections. It is only natural that after listening to the lengthy debate he has lost track of those arguments. But he lost track of what I consider to be the real objections, and it is for that reason I speak now, in an effort to draw those to his attention. Because I do believe that, in a house, composed of reasonable men, it should be possible to come to an early conclusion on this matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I want to refer to the minister's statement to be found at page 5382 of

Defence Production Act Hansard. And this is the whole crux of the situation, so far as I can see:
If it had been suggested earlier that it would relieve people's minds-and I think it would have relieved the minds of the Social Crediters-to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered. But we would have done it with full knowledge that another extension would be necessary, because the very development work on the supersonic planes I am talking about is a six-year program, and I am satisfied the guided missile program will go far beyond that period.
Note these words:
If it had been suggested earlier that it would relieve people's minds-and I think it would have relieved the minds of the Social Crediters-to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered.
Those are rather amazing words. Surely the minister has not forgotten the earlier part of the debate, when the whole argument at the resolution stage was that a time limit should be put on the bill. In order that there may be no misunderstanding let me go back to the month of March, and quote the words of the leader of this group, as they appear at page 2001 of Hansard:

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Would the minister not say that it might be wise to make it mandatory upon the government to have this legislation submitted for review at regular intervals? I think the idea suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is an excellent one, whereby the minister could consider including in the act some provision to make it mandatory upon the government to submit it to the house for review, let us say in three or four years, or whatever he feels desirable.
The words my leader used were:
-in three or four years, or whatever he feels desirable.
The minister now says that if we had made a suggestion of a limit of five years, it might have been taken into consideration. Well, we did made a suggestion of "three or four years, or whatever time he feels desirable" -that is any time the minister might consider was advisable. In the light of that statement I do not think the minister can say at this time that we did not make a suggestion that a time limit be put in. If hon. members will turn to the next page 2002 they will find that the leader of this group when speaking on this very point had this to say:
That is exactly what it would be, and that appears to us to be the meaning of it. Surely it would be a simple matter for the Prime Minister to say "We shall give consideration to such a provision in the act and will bring something in." That is all we are asking. What about it, Mr. Chairman? May I ask the Prime Minister if he is prepared to give consideration to such a provision?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and
Commerce has already stated that the government would give consideration to the views which have been expressed here in that regard.

In the light of that statement the Minister of Defence Production cannot say today that we did not make a recommendation for a time limit. Yet he says that if a recommendation had been made this government would have been prepared to give it consideration. So I say that in view of the fact that that recommendation was made, in view of the fact that the minister now says that had that recommendation been made he would have given it consideration, I think that the minister might very well even at this late date give consideration to that point and suggest that a time limit be inserted in the bill.
Up to the end of the resolution stage I would say that the government had adopted a reasonable attitude. They had listened to the arguments of the opposition. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production had stated that they would give consideration to the proposals of the opposition. Then on June 7 the minister made it clear that they were not prepared to act along the lines suggested by the opposition, and he is reported on page 4510 of Hansard as saying:
Such is not the case, and it is in the light of present-day circumstances that I am compelled to recommend the continuation of the Defence Production Act in its present form.
And then on page 4511:
Either you have a defence production act with these powers, and all these powers, or you have no act at all.
The minister made it quite clear that he was not prepared to accept any amendment to place a termination date on the powers in the act. If the Minister of Defence Production still has some doubt in his mind as to what I have just said, I would refer him to what the leader of this group said on June 8 as reported on page 4550 of Hansard:
We believe that this parliament is the repository of all the sovereign authority of the people of Canada and therefore we have no right to dispose permanently of any of those powers. Even if we hand over powers only on a temporary basis we are obligated not to do so without a provision for terminating the grant or the requirement that parliament be given an opportunity to review and to make full scrutiny of the way in which the powers have been used.
That is what we want now. I think our request is reasonable and fair. What is the right thing for us to do on this motion for second reading?
I think the right thing for us to do would be to support those things which the minister requires and which are right, but also to serve warning that when the bill is in committee we will move for the deletion of clause 2, which repeals section 41 of the act, and offer an amendment to make it mandatory upon the government to bring the act back to this house for complete periodic review and scrutiny. We are unalterably opposed, may I repeat, to the granting to the minister and his department of unusual powers on a permanent basis, and against that we will continue to fight.

In the light of what was said at the resolution stage; in the light of what was said by the leader of this group at that time and by other members of the opposition the Minister of Defence Production cannot say today that a recommendation to put in a time limit was not made in the early part of the debate. It was made time and again; it was repeated day after day. In the light of that I think the minister should be prepared to give further consideration to that point and should say now that he will be prepared to put in a five-year limit so that the act can be brought back to parliament. He has stated that if that recommendation had been made by the opposition in the early stages of the debate it might have been possible to do it. In view of the fact that he now finds that it was made I think in fairness and without having to back down in any way the minister might well say, "All right, I missed that point, I am quite prepared to put in that clause with a five-year limit to the powers."
I would say that the present debate is an example of parliament at its very worst. After all, we are supposed to be reasonable men, we are supposed to reason out things rather than having long-winded debates using a lot of language which is not always complimentary, the kind of language that Mr. Speaker thinks would be better left off the record. Surely we should be able to deal with matters without that kind of thing happening. In view of the fact that the minister has made it clear that he would have been willing to take action on a time limit it seems to me that what we need at this stage is just a little co-operation between the government and the opposition.
I am reminded of a picture which used to be circulated in the early days about the benefits of co-operation. This was circulated mainly throughout western Canada. It showed two stacks of hay between which two donkeys were tied together. Both donkeys wanted to feed but they both insisted on pulling in opposite directions. The result was that neither got what he wanted. I am sure both the government and the opposition have the same objective, the best defence we can get for Canada. We find that there is a certain difficulty between the government and the opposition. Would it not be wiser if they turned around and instead of pulling against each other both tried to go toward that objective? The minister may say that this comparison is wrong because in the case of the picture the two donkeys were evenly matched whereas the government can be said to be the larger of the two donkeys and able to pull the opposition over. I agree that there is some truth in the argument of the
Defence Production Act government being the larger of the two and that eventually they can force the opposition to give way.
The minister is a reasonable man and it seems to me that in the light of the statement he made on Tuesday he should be prepared to put in a five-year limit. On page 4511 of Hansard of June 7 the minister referred to the difficulty of making the act permanent and the powers temporary, and I quote what he said:
In order to require a review by parliament and attach to it legal consequences it would be necessary, for example, to provide that the act would expire at a stated time unless reviewed and reapproved and re-enacted before the expiration of that time. This obviously was not the intent indicated by the request put forward by the hon. members.
Let me interject there. It is true that we said we would go along with the minister and make the Defence Production Act permanent; it was merely the powers we wanted to terminate. If, on the other hand, it is not possible to make the powers temporary then we feel that the whole act should be terminated at the end of five years and re-enacted. The minister pointed out that apparently that was the attitude of justice, and he goes on to say:
Suggestions of the Department of Justice to achieve the results desired by the hon. members were along these lines, as in each case they required that certain sections of the act be singled out at this time and designated as clauses which should expire at a given date in the future.
I would have thought that the Department of Justice could have redrafted the act in such a way as to keep the powers under the act apart from the rest of the act. However, if it is not possible to do that, then the act should be brought back and re-enacted. Personally I am quite prepared to support the Defence Production Act if it is needed. The minister has quite convinced me that these powers are needed at the present time. I am not objecting to that, but not even the minister knows what the situation will be five years from now. We all hope that eventually there may be some agreement reached between the nations of the world. The United Nations are working toward that end. We hope it may be possible to have disarmament. Perhaps in five years' time we shall have achieved that goal.
I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare would not say he is such a pessimist that he does not think we can come to an agreement. Possibly an agreement can be reached by that time. If it were reached by that time, then the minister himself would admit that those powers would no longer be needed.

I wonder whether we could not have a section put in the act under section 41 which would state that instead of this act expiring in 1956 it would expire in 1961. Then, in the spring of 1961 we could review it again. If the situation warranted further extension, the extension could be made.
Let me give the minister an example of another act in which this is done. This is a totally different act, but its powers are very widespread. Take the wheat board act. Part II of the wheat board act, under section 23, is repealed in 1957. I am sure the minister will agree with me that the farmers are not asking for the act to be repealed. They would like to see that section eliminated entirely and part II made a permanent part of the act. Under section 23 of the act, part II is repealed in 1957. I do not think the minister believes-I certainly do not-that we are going to do away with part II in 1957. There would be a tremendous protest from the farm organizations if the government decided to do that. The farmers have not asked for section 23. The minister feels it is only right that where wide powers are given to the wheat board under that act they should be subject to review from time to time. Therefore, the minister, in this instance, has insisted upon putting a time limit in the act, a time limit ot four years. At the end of that time the act has to come back to parliament for review. Surely, if in the case of the control over elevators it is necessary periodically to bring the act back to parliament for review, then in a case like this, where the powers are so much greater, it should also be a matter of wisdom to bring the act back to parliament to allow parliament to decide whether or not those powers should be extended.
Perhaps I should read the amendment moved by the Conservatives to the bill before us:
That Bill No. 256, an act to amend the Defence Production Act, be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to examine and report upon the advisability of
(a)	placing the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis and conferring on the department such powers as ought to be of a continuing nature; and
(b)	conferring for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament, such additional powers as may be strictly necessary in the light of the existing world conditions.
I presume that (b) which reads:
conferring for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament,-


means for one year or for whatever time parliament should see fit to extend the bill. If the bill is to be left as it is we shall support the amendment. In the light of what the minister said on page 5382 of Hansard we would much rather that the minister would state to the house that the government are prepared to put a five-year limit on it. Let me read again what the minister said at that time:
If it had been suggested earlier that it would relieve people's minds-and I think it would have relieved the minds of the Social Crediters-to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered.
In the light of that statement, and in the light of the evidence I have now put on the record, I say, without the shadow of a doubt, that that suggestion was put on the record, and that therefore the minister now, without losing face at all, could very well say he would be prepared to put a five-year limit on the act. In which case we would support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just three things to say. In order that nobody on the other side may have any misconception, may I say that, just like every other Liberal in this house, I am 100 per cent behind the minister.
The first thing I want to say, Mr. Speaker, is that the rule on repetition should be watched closely. For my own amusement I have at times chalked down the number of repetitions that have taken place. It would surprise the opposition if they could have a little look at that record. The rule should be observed because I should like to see any member of the opposition, who can stand up and speak to the bill, say something altogether his own and not repeat anything. I do not think it is fair to keep on repeating, because these repetitions are costly to the taxpayers.
The second thing is this. I remember that during the second world war we were caught unprepared and that the government chose the present minister as minister of munitions and supply. I can remember that very distinctly because I knew what the minister was doing. The statement that came from all corners of the opposition was, "Too little, too late." I do not think anybody will doubt that. I can remember when he organized the best brains of Canada to get the best tools for the air force, the army and the navy. He did an outstanding job for us. Then it was "Too little and too late."
The minister shows his common sense when he says that he is not going to be caught again in that way, whether there is going to be a war or not. I myself think there is not

going to be a war, but he is not going to be caught again with his hands tied and to hear the cry "Too little and too late." I wonder what the opposition would say if he were caught again; but he is going to be prepared.
The third thing has to do with the right to strike. Anybody who works for the minister is so well treated that he does not want to strike. Those of us who come from the head of the lakes know-and I have used this before, and I shall use it again-that he was the only man in Canada who selected for his staff the best engineers and the best assistants that he could get. When there was no more work for them to do he told them to come in and play as they liked, and their salaries would be paid just the same. I wish to heaven our industries were headed by men like the minister. If they were, there would be no unemployment and no relief. He knew how to treat men; he knew how to treat all those who worked in his departments, and I have known many of them. They would like to continue to work for him. Therefore he wants the people who work in his department to be sure that the department is not limited to five, six or 10 years, but is like any other department.
I am going to support this bill, I do not care how long the discussion takes. If it takes until Christmas or until Easter I am going to stay with it, because I think it is right.

The Minister of Defence Production referred to it the other day, and it was referred to in some of the newspapers as if that in itself was a horrible thing to take place in parliament. I am not sure that it has been entirely unknown in this forum previously, Mr. Speaker. I do not think this forum is like a court room where one is always cold, logical and analytically correct. I think even the Minister of Defence Production himself will admit that on occasion he has indulged in something closely resembling exaggeration. We have always had the most roseate views of the future which he has to meet next year by even greater roseate views of a further future rather than perhaps looking back at the past. But in any event, as I said, I do not think exaggeration is a matter which is entirely unknown to anybody in this house. I do not think it weakens the position that anyone may have taken here to say, "You have indulged in exaggeration".

After all, if you are starting out on a road, up on the hill or on the mountain top, you may know where that road is going. You know that the road is going down over slippery precipices into ravines, swamps, morasses and into a bog. While it may be that you are standing up in clear air and on firm ground where you are at the moment, if you know where the road is going I do not think it is any exaggeration to refer to the swamps, the ravines and the precipices over which you are going to go rather than to the relatively calm air in which you are standing at the moment.
That is the situation with respect to the opposition in dealing with this bill. On the face of it, it is an innocuous bill with two sections; it is a simple piece of legislation. But we feel that it is starting on a road which has been well marked by history, one which all of us know, and one which takes us down off the hill of parliamentary supremacy, over slippery precipices and down into the swamp where parliament has lost control and where there is autocracy or where something else of that kind has taken place. It is true that it is the beginning of the road, but I say that it is not an exaggeration to paint what happens on the road when one is dealing with the matter. That is all that the opposition has tried to do in dealing with this matter.
There are other matters to which the right hon. gentleman referred when speaking the other day-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock I was referring to the statements which have sometimes been made here by the minister that the opposition was dealing with exaggerations in discussing this bill. I questioned that fact and pointed out that when one saw the road on which one was entering one could be forgiven for discussing the latter part of that road which perhaps you could not see clearly but which you knew was there as well as the part on which you were starting. In that connection I should like to refer to the speech of the minister delivered last Tuesday, the 28th of June. As found at page 5378 of Hansard, the minister, in referring to his powers and the

fact that it had not always been necessary to use them officially, went on to say:
We said to the steel companies that we must have our steel requirements in the interests of national defence and that they would have to set aside or postpone civilian orders in order to give us this steel when we needed it for this most essential defence project. That has been done and there has been no need for formal government action.
Then the minister went on to say:
As I say, that procedure is one way of handling a well-disciplined munitions industry.
I want to emphasize that phrase particularly-"that is one way of handling a well-disciplined munitions industry". I remember a gentleman who achieved power in another country years ago by the name of Mussolini who said that he needed to inspire more discipline in the workers. We know of another gentleman who achieved power in another country, and I know people of this country who praised Hitler because they said he was inspiring discipline in the workers. I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that you can search the Hansards of all of the parliaments of the free countries of the world and you will not find a phrase equivalent to that which I have just read to you, that this procedure is one way of handling a well-disciplined munitions industry.
Of course, there is the discipline and then there is the carrot on the other end because a little later the minister says, as found at page 5879:
-I have never known Canadian industry to see the Department of Defence Production in a jam without feeling willing to do whatever was needed to make their contribution to solving the dilemma.
So you have the handling of a well-disciplined industry by this legislation and then, as I said, you have the holding out of the carrot when the minister says that, after all, they are good, and he has never known them to leave him in a jam. I wonder where coercion ceases and co-operation begins. That would be an interesting question and one to which I think more attention should be paid than we have had so far.
We are now going to have this same system applied to parliament, Mr. Speaker, because when you turn to page 5382 you see that the minister says:
The situation has reached the point where the government must insist that this legislation be passed.
We have got a well-disciplined industry and now we are going to have a well-disciplined parliament. That is what that means. It cannot mean anything else if words mean anything. Therefore when one says we are indulging in exaggeration I say it is not
Defence Production Act exaggeration at all. One takes the words of the minister the other day and, as I said, I challenge him, I challenge any hon. member of the house, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) or anyone else, to find an equivalent statement in any Hansard of any parliament in the free world.
But it is so reminiscent of those things which we have known before. The minister says in dealing with parliament that "the situation has reached the point". What situation? What situation has reached the point? Parliamentary debate. There is no change in the international situation. How has the international situation changed since last March? The legislation is effective until July of 1956. Why has the situation reached the point where the government must insist that this legislation be passed? Only one point has been reached. Members of the House of Commons have been indulging in orderly debate, but by doing that we arrive at a point where the government must insist that this legislation be passed.
As far as we are concerned, we deny emphatically that there is any suggestion of exaggeration in this matter, and we welcome this debate. A lot of us have been glancing through Hansard in the last few days. I remember Sir Robert Borden once referred to a session of parliament by saying that the snows of the late spring were falling when parliament assembled and the snows of the early fall had fallen before parliament prorogued. That is a picture which I suggest the seriousness of this debate would warrant. If that has to happen then we feel we are justified in our action and we welcome this debate.
As far as we know, officially debate on the bill is only going to be for this day, although we understand from information we have obtained that it may go on for three days or so. I am glad of that. I think the house leader has shown-I do not think Machiavellian would be out of order- a shrewd sense of timing in dealing with debates generally. They start, then they are broken off, they start again, and then they are broken off. Altogether we do not usually get continuity of debate. We would have preferred to have continuity so that this situation could have been presented clearly to the public over a matter of several days instead of debate going on for one day, then breaking off for a week, and then going on for another day.
But if we are now to have the opportunity of dealing with this matter fully for three or four days I am sure we of the opposition welcome it, and I do not think that in the end you are going to find that parliament is

Defence Production Act disciplined. I think that probably what the minister would like to do is discipline some of his colleagues in the cabinet rather than discipline parliament itself. I am not just sure where he wants the discipline applied, but in any event that is the background of this debate, that is why we are here at the moment, and that is why we intend to stay here until this debate is concluded. I can tell you now that is not going to be within a short time.
In his speech the other day the minister gave various reasons why the legislation had to be extended. I must say the ground has shifted, I think, from that which he took in March when he said it was because of the emergency, the crisis with which we were confronted. Last Tuesday he gave several reasons as to why the bill had to be passed at this time. I am going to refer briefly to them.
In the first place, he gave us a horrendous tale about the A. V. Roe expenditures, and the fact that he lost a great deal of sleep at night because between $30 million and $40 million had been invested in that plant and he was not sure we were going to get it back. He said that we had paid $122 million before a single plane had been developed. The minister went on to say at page 5382 of Hansard that the only purpose of this bill which we are discussing was to protect the taxpayer of Canada. That is bringing it down to quite a different plane from that upon which it was put in March when this bill was necessary to protect the liberties of the free world. Now, it is necessary to protect the taxpayers of Canada. He uses the $122 million as an example of why it is necessary to have this bill. Well, $122 million, as we know, Mr. Speaker, is a large sum of money. I am willing to admit that I am very much of a layman when it comes to the construction of aeroplanes. I do not venture to give any expert opinion on it whatever, except that which one has read in the newspapers or has heard from people who are associated with the industry.
Then, the minister said he had to change the management. After he entered into this agreement, he found something was wrong and after he had spent $40 million he had to threaten to use his powers in order to save the $40 million. He said that was why he needed the bill. I would suggest to the minister that the best way to avoid that is not to enter into any such agreement at all. I do not think the taxpayers of Canada expect us to indulge in all kinds of experimentation and pioneering work that call for the powers of a czar to carry them through. This is a relatively small country with a population of

14 or 15 million. We are associated with the United States, with Great Britain and with France, so I doubt if it is necessary for us to go ahead and-develop prototypes for various aeroplanes or the other mechanics of war, unless there is the closest co-operation and consultation between the various countries involved. Certainly, from some of the other examples which the minister gave I would not suggest that we need to do that.
Surely, the United States, France and Australia have been willing to enter into plans for the construction of aeroplanes by licence from Great Britain. Surely, the engineering facilities of that country, the technical skill and the production lines of the United States should be able, and be expected, to take up a good part of this load instead of our having to pioneer in these fields and risk hundreds of millions of dollars to the point where you have to give a minister the powers of a czar in case he enters into such agreement and might lose the taxpayers' money. Frankly, I do not believe the people of Canada expect that of this government. They expect us to do our share. They expect us to develop where we can and to produce what we can, but certainly it should be done in co-operation with the other powers rather than by doing it on our own.
The minister gave us another example over which he says he is losing sleep and that was the supersonic aeroplane. He says we are going to spend six years in developing a supersonic aeroplane. At page 5380 of Hansard he said that we had already invested $30 million in that project, and before we get through the investment will run over $100 million. I am not saying the minister was attempting to mislead anyone, but certainly as I read his speech I gathered the impression that we were pioneering again in this field. We were developing a supersonic aeroplane and supersonic engines, as he said, and that we would invest over $100 million in that one project. If we were successful we would get our money back and if we were not successful we would not get our money back. Certainly, as I said, he created the impression in my mind that this was something new, something revolutionary, and therefore we were going to lead the free world in this matter.
I was rather surprised last night, Mr. Speaker, having read the minister's speech over carefully several times during the day, to find upon reading the Sunday edition of the New York Times for a little relaxation that on page 16 they refer to several squadrons of supersonic planes which are now in operation in the United States. As I have said, I am wondering again why we should

be pioneering in the development of this if other countries have already achieved what the minister is going to try to do at the expense of so many sleepless nights and at the risk of several hundred millions of dollars.
The minister told us too that he needed these powers because of guided missiles. He says we are going to spend a great deal of money in that field in order to develop guided missiles. On page 5380 of Hansard, he says that this is the field in which no country has achieved very much as yet. I am sure that is going to be complimentary to our United States friends who have been boasting-I will not say boasting; that is perhaps an unfortunate phrase-who have been telling us of the great achievements they have made in that field. The minister probably would not accept the statement of Stewart Alsop in his writings about what the United States has done in that field, but perhaps he will accept what Hanson Baldwin says. He says the United States is leading the world and is making such terrific progress that soon the problem will be solved. I suggest to the minister that rather than have sleepless nights and waste so many millions of dollars we should manufacture these articles under a licence from the United States. At least, he will save some sleep and we will save some money and we will not need this bill.
Another example he gave-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Why bother with any defence production at all?

speechtext:
Why bother with defence production at all? Bother with it just the same as other countries are doing, and do it in co-operation and co-ordination. We have said there was some co-operation and co-ordination between the free nations of the world, and the Minister of Defence Production would have you believe that there is none. I can tell you this, sir: if there was one speech which would be encouraging to the enemy it was the speech made by the minister the other day when he said that Canada was pioneering in every field to develop these things and until they are developed apparently the free nations are not going to have them.
I am not unconscious of the fact the minister once said that if the Department of National Defence told him to get a gold-plated piano, he would get one. It may be that they have told him to get a gold-plated piano and I am suggesting that he buy the piano from some country that has developed it now rather than impose the developmental and manufacturing costs on this country.
Defence Production Act

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: I am glad to know the policy of the Conservative party.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We have been trying to impress upon you the policy of the party for quite some time, but you would not listen.
Again, we are told about the development of this anti-aircraft gun and we are led to wonder whether this is co-operation or megalomania. Apparently the suggestion is we are to do everything on our own and we are not to take any advice or accept any co-operation from any other country. It would appear that this is the sole justification for the bill, to save the taxpayers' money. We are told about this naval anti-aircraft gun. We have to develop and pioneer that, too, and it is going to cost us millions and millions of dollars. One would have thought that the navies of the United States and Great Britain, which are somewhat larger than ours, would have developed such a gun. Our navy has been essentially an antisubmarine navy and one of the most efficient in the world. If this gun is as powerful as the minister would have us believe, then I do not believe any of our little frigates or corvettes would be able to mount it anyway. I do not know whether they could mount it on the William Carson, which has no point of anchorage.
Anyway, those are some of the examples. Those are the arguments which the right hon. gentleman used the other day. And I say frankly that if those are the only justifications he has to offer, then certainly he has not advanced any reason for our accepting clause 2 of the bill. And I am beginning to wonder if we should not reconsider it even with respect to clause 1, because if he is indulging in all these experiments, then it might be necessary, if we are to have proper co-ordination and co-operation, that we review that decision.
But, be that as it may, as I said, it was not the picture of co-operation, co-ordination and integrated development between the nations of the world, which I expected was taking place-and which I think frankly is taking place. I wonder if there was not some exaggeration on his part, and if he did not develop those arguments because he felt that he had to make as strong an argument as possible, and because he felt he was alone in this debate, and did not have the support that he should have, and that he was putting forth an argument that would not appeal to the great majority of the people of Canada.
Then, of course, he brings in the mid-Canada line. He says that this bill is necessary in connection with the production of steel for the construction of the mid-Canada line.
5638	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act Mr. Howe (Port Arthur): Why build the mid-Canada line?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Somebody has asked that question; I am not asking it. But I will say this, that the minister reminds me of a story once told me by a predecessor of yours, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. E. N. Rhodes. He at one time occupied the chair you now occupy, sir, and he told me about a trip he had made to Great Britain during the first war, and of a conversation he had with the director of the Armstrong company in Great Britain. He said, "I suppose you have solved all your problems?" The manager said, "No, there are two yet to solve. We have to solve the problem of a shell which will pierce any armour plate, and we have to solve the problem of constructing armour plate that will resist any shell."
I suppose that is the problem confronting the minister. He says he is building supersonic planes and guided missiles which will jump so high and so fast that no radar screen can get them, while at the same time he is building radar screens that are to detect those planes. And that is probably necessary in this day and age.
But I do suggest this, that for the minister to tell us that this bill is now necessary, or an extension of it, for the construction of the mid-Canada line is certainly a confession of failure on his part. Because, while none of us knows how far construction has gone, yet certainly there has been enough in the press of this country and enough statements made to leave any person in Canada- and this has been done by the department as well as by the press-with the impression that it is well under construction.
We have this act which has another year before it expires; and for any responsible man or any irresponsible man, for the minister or any member in the house, to stand up and give the construction of the mid-Canada line as the reason for the extension of these powers for another five years is, I suggest, an insult to the intelligence of this House of Commons, and is certainly one of the greatest points of weakness, in so far as arguments for the necessity of this bill are concerned.

[Mr. Nowlan.)

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The minister is not getting much out of the debate, so far, and certainly he has not contributed much to it.
Then, again, he talks about the stresses and strains of today, and increased emergency. After all, we do have the statement in the press of yesterday where Sir Anthony Eden states that when the big four meet at the summit next week-that is, Sir Anthony Eden, the President of the United States, the President of France and the Russian representative-there will be a positive suggestion with respect to disarmament. I am not saying that the suggestion will be accepted. But that statement is recorded in the press, as a dispatch from London appearing in yesterday's New York Times.
I do say that there is no increased tension. Nothing has arisen since March which could possibly justify the extension of this bill for a period of five years, as was suggested by the minister. Somebody told me the other day, someone who has been around here for a long time, that this situation reminds him of what took place in 1916, when there was a very strong and self-willed minister, who was then minister of national defence and also perhaps the equivalent of the minister of defence production. That minister had difficulty with the minister of finance of that day over the way in which he was spending money. The man told me that a great deal went on behind the scenes, but he pointed out that there was then a strong prime minister in charge of the situation. At that time one minister had to retire, and the whole matter was put on a different basis.
That is an historical allusion which comes to mind, and which was pointed out by someone who has been an observer of debates and of parliamentary procedure for many years. Certainly there is something in common between the situation we have today and the difficulty that arose in another government, and at the time of another war, when Sir Robert Borden was prime minister, and when there was a minister of finance who apparently disagreed with another minister. The prime minister of that day had to intervene and deal with the matter so as to preserve the orderly processes of government. The self-willed minister went out, while the minister of finance received the support of the prime minister and was carried on.
I notice today in the report of the dominion fuel board that they say there is a necessity for creating a fuel policy, if the coal industry of this country is to be saved. I am wondering if there are not many things which should be engaging the attention of the minister, as well as these matters to which he

drew our attention the other day. There are many other problems in this country that require his attention, and to which he could give a solution. I do suggest co-operation in those matters is required, rather than going ahead on experimental lines as he is in this instance.
And again-and this is a rather amazing thing-we are told about the great emergency, and the necessity for these powers. Yet the press have suggested to us, and we have read apparently about differences in the Department of National Defence-differences over some sort of policy-but there does not seem to be any sign of emergency, so far as national defence is concerned.
If there is any great emergency in this country and if there is any reason for these statements which have been made, and the heads which have rolled because of disapproval of the statements made, then one would think that there would be some necessity for action in that department. Yet you have one going ahead serenely on his own and the other apparently demanding further and greater powers for the emergency.
I do not believe, frankly, that the arguments which were advanced the other day by the right hon. gentleman give support to his claim that this bill should be extended. I do not think they do that at all. I do not think that is the reason for it. I think that everyone must feel that there is something more here than meets the eye. Without indulging in any political gossip whatsoever, I have the feeling that there is an internecine feud somewhere, and that this matter is being fought through on the basis of stubbornness and self-will rather than because of any necessity for it in principle.
Certain people, having taken a position, will not back down. I know that we used to read in our nature book about the old head of the tribe, or whoever it may be-the old bull at the head of the herd-who would not give way until he had done battle with someone younger, and one or the other would be forced out.
We wonder if we are not seeing an internecine feud like that at the present time and, in parliament, in which gouging and goring is going on. I am not sure whether the battle-scarred old bull or the young bull will win, but as far as we of the opposition are concerned we intend to see that parliament will not lose.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the election ballots are counted there is always one party in power with the other party in opposition. I have always been imbued with the idea that the party
Defence Production Act in opposition has a very definite task to perform, that is to criticize the government when they feel it is in the public interest to do so. We are often asked why we do not suggest something constructive. Those who ask that question do not realize that if we suggested these constructive ideas those in the government would soon tell the suggesters that they had nothing to do with the running of the country, that their role was purely and simply that of opposition critics.
We all know that this world has been through some trying experiences. We have had two terrible wars and anyone with any degree of intelligence knows that when we entered the first world war in 1914 we were inadequately equipped to meet the German hordes. Many lives were lost because of lack of equipment. At the time of the second world war I did not happen to be a member of parliament but there are many others sitting here who were in the same position. But I say that those who were in the trenches in the first world war were told that they could shoot only so many shots from their rifles, that there were only so many 16-pounder shells a day. Those men had to serve time and a half overtime at $1.10 a day in order to defend their portion of the trenches because there were no reinforcements available.
There was a Conservative government in power, and to say the least they fell down on the job badly and it cost thousands of young Canadian lives. It was not only the Canadian government that fell down, the British government also fell down. After that war we all said that we would never find ourselves unprepared against an enemy; but along came 1936 and 1937 and we heard of a man named Hitler who had aeroplanes galore, who had underground hangars and all kinds of equipment and yet the people were assured by the parliament of Great Britain and this parliament that we had it in the bag, that we had something up our sleeves to meet this man Hitler who had all the necessities to carry on a successful war.
What did we discover? In 1939 we discovered that we had very few aeroplanes and practically no anti-aircraft guns. The loss of life of peoples of the British empire was appalling and unnecessary. There is not a part of the British empire which does not realize the necessity for preparation, and certainly not the Conservative party in the House of Commons today. Ninety per cent of all members of the Conservative party served in one war or the other. These men have suffered and have seen other people suffer through lack of preparation.
Men who have seen such things would be the last in the world not to stand firm behind any government or any member of a
5640	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act government in demanding common-sense preparations for adequate defence needs. We in this party know that we need munitions. We are not children; we realize and believe in our hearts that the Russians are up to their old tricks. Nobody on this side of the house, no one in the ranks of the Liberal party, or among even our friends here in the C.C.F. can possibly conceive that the Russians are going to give up their grasp on China, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Bulgaria and all those countries. We are not sure what they are trying to do, but I think we can be sure that in the back of their minds they mean nothing less than the destruction of the people on this side of the iron curtain by insidious methods of working through labour and creating discontent all over the world. We saw their tactics here in Ottawa when spies were discovered, even one member of the House of Commons. They are finding that more effective and easier than actual war.
They may be ready to give up Austria and give her back her rights, and they may be even willing to let West Germany and East Germany unite. I hope they do for the sake of East Germany. But we must remember that they have indoctrinated those people with communist principles. The young element in East Germany have been indoctrinated. Any person who has been there and who has studied the situation knows full well that if tomorrow the Russians said that they were going to let East Germany unite with West Germany they would feel that the younger element had been sufficiently educated to create devastation and destruction far greater than they could bring about with war.
West Germany has recently been given permission to rearm. A very eminent and cultured university graduate, a great industrialist of Germany, said to me that if they had 900,000 armed men, if Germany were united with that force of well-trained Germans the Russians would not dare use the atomic bomb. He said that even with the 20 per cent of the people who want Russia to remain in East Germany they could still defeat the Russians.
