speechtext: It would not matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
It would not make any difference but I would like to know. I am saying these things because the minister must realize that we are just as loyal to our country as he ever will be and that we 

realize the necessity for immediate action in preparation for defence. We will not tolerate under any circumstances any party in Canada saying to the government that they will not permit the proper thing to be done at the proper prices and in the time necessary. The minister would have a 100 per cent unanimous vote of this house if he would lay his cards on the table. He would find that there would be nothing lacking. Anyone who with his own eyes has seen what happened knows the price we paid for a lack of preparation. He will know what the mothers, the fathers, the husbands and the wives had to suffer. We have been through two great wars.
The trouble in Great Britain and in Canada in the past has been that they did not think it was necessary to tell the people of the necessity for preparation. They were afraid to tell the people that it would be necessary to increase taxes in order to defend the country. They did not want to do that because some of their members might lose their seats in the House of Commons. They were afraid to tell the truth and shame the devil. There is no man who did not wonder why we were not better advised as everyday civilians. Our forefathers defended this country against an enemy who tried to take it over. They shed their blood on the banks of the St. Lawrence river, and I shall do it if necessary. We are associated with a neighbour to the south, and nobody in the world can have a finer neighbour. They have proven that, beyond any shadow of a doubt. So far as our defence is concerned they are part and parcel of it. We can rely on them and they can rely on us. We require every sinew of our strength to meet the enemy who does not mean peace, who does not mean to give up his control over the countries he has overrun today. It may mean war. That may be his second decision. We must be prepared for that.
I have had dealings with the minister outside the House of Commons. He is a man who comes from a great university. He came here and he entered a great university. He tackled the business of the construction of elevators at the head of the lakes, and made a huge success of it where other people had failed. There is no doubt of the ability of the minister in his own line of endeavour. There is no doubt about the contribution he made to this country. He has been so successful that he has shone brighter than most of the cabinet ministers. They think he is God himself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: So does he.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I have often asked for reasonable things. When I had evidence to show that a particular thing was necessary, I have never had a kinder reception or a more tolerant hearing than I have received from the minister. If I was right I received concessions. I say to the minister that none of us here is trying to upset the applecart, to leave this country unprepared. Since that is how we all feel, we think we have a right to believe in this great over-all picture. We also feel that there is power in parliament. There is a democratic form of government here so long as there is an opposition. I cannot say that much for the Senate. But here we still have the privilege of electing men to parliament, and no matter how small the numbers may be, those men will be admired if they stand on their feet and if they believe in what they say, and if they say to the House of Commons, "This is what we believe in, for the following reasons". Surely that is not unreasonable. Surely the word "filibuster" should not be used from now on. Irrespective of politics, I believe there are men here who must say to themselves: These people have a just cause, they are carrying out their function as an opposition. It is a good argument. Some good points have been brought out here, and the minister must say to himself, "If I were sitting in opposition, I might have the same thoughts myself, if I were to carry out my duty to the people who sent me here."
I can also realize the minister's apprehension, because I believe he feels as I do with regard to the enemy. He might strike without notice. He is in a preferred position with respect to making decisions on defence. He may build aircraft and lose $100 million. There were times when we would have been better off if we had lost a few million dollars rather than create the position of blocking the path of the enemy with practically nothing else but human flesh. Do not deny it.
The Conservatives were in power during the first war; the Liberals were in power during the second war. Canada was proud to call itself a nation in 1914. I had the idea that the Canadian army could whip the German army with one hand tied behind its back. Do not forget the Niobe; that was our navy. We volunteered. We went to Valcartier. The bands were playing. We could not get there fast enough. After being there for a short time we thought we would never get out of the place.
We remember the recruiting in 1937. There were so many recruits that they would not take a man in the Canadian army unless he was five feet nine inches tall. I began to
Defence Production Act think that the Japanese would not have a very large army if the soldiers had to be five feet nine, but those little fellows gave a very good account of themselves. Before the war was over, we were taking boys five feet two, five feet three, and 16 to 17 years of age. It was a great honour to be enlisted in the army in 1914. I remember going to my family doctor and saying to him: "Do not turn me down." He pushed me in without even examining me. I will never forgive him as long as I live. I often wish he could have found a bunion or something, but unfortunately he did not.
These are serious times, gentlemen. The opposition have to formulate opinions. We want to go along with the government when we know what is going on. We also want the government to say to us: "We hope and pray that these powers will not be necessary. We do not want to take power away from the House of Commons and make it like the Canadian Senate today. We at least want to come back to you people in three years. What man in the Conservative opposition today, or in any party, for that matter, would refuse the government's request if the Liberal party came to the house and asked for a renewal of those powers, if they were necessary? I think it is a gross insult to the country. What man here would not give the government power for three years, two years or 10 years to defend the people whom they have sworn to defend? That is why I am speaking. I represent the constituency of Simcoe North, of which I am very proud. The men and women of that constituency volunteered for service in both wars. They are people who love their country; but above all they expect Julian Ferguson to come to parliament and make a plea on their behalf, as he sees the situation.
I believe I am speaking for them, and if at the next election they believe that I have not spoken for them they will have the privilege of telling me so. That is democracy. But I say to every member on the government benches, and to the minister: please have confidence in your fellow members of the House of Commons, and remember that united we stand, divided we fall in any crisis, and that blood courses through the veins of the members of the Liberal party in the same way as it does in the veins of the people of the opposition.
It is my opinion, and I am sure it is the minister's, that we face a terrible situation; but why in the world would the minister ask for powers for an unlimited time? Why ignore the powers of debate? Let us have a discussion openly and on behalf of the people with members of the press gallery

Defence Production Act present to take down our words, right or wrong, and publish them across the country for the information of the people. Do not give the power to any individual or to any government that is in office, and leave the crumbs of the pie to be consumed in the house.
I ask the minister and the members of the House of Commons to give this more considered thought, because it is our duty. The inventors of the world are great men. When they say that a thing is perfect they often find that they have to give it a second look and change their minds. These are the greatest men in the world, who created all the marvellous things we have today. They may say a thing is perfect, and three seconds later they say it is not and it must be improved. They are men who change their minds. We do not think they are incapable or incompetent because of that. We do not lose our regard for them. The minister has had appeals from people who are not against him. I can assure him of that but I want one thing to be clear, irrespective of who the minister may be who may be forcing through something that is voted on now or something that is consented to now and who thinks these powers are necessary. I for one also think these powers are necessary. I believe in them 100 per cent. I believe we are treading as dangerous ground as any that we have ever trod in the past, and that the more the Russians can lull us to sleep, the more they will do so. We do not need to go back very far to see what they permitted all over this world. I refer to persecution and massacres almost beyond the imagination of man. These are the people-hundreds of millions of them- with whom we are dealing. They will use any tactics in the world.
Let us be united. We can talk frivolously politically. We can talk on the hustings about this or that minor thing, about our getting a new dam, a better road, a new post office or some such thing. These are trivialities compared with the subject that is now being discussed in this house. It is a subject upon which we should all be at one. If I were to ask my party, if it wanted plainly to show its position, to stand up and say whether they are 100 per cent behind the effort for creating positive protection and contributing along with all other countries outside of the iron curtain, I would say that every one of them would stand on his feet and do so or resign from parliament if you want them to. I plead with you and say, "Please carry on the democratic form of government, Mr. Minister, and say you will come back to parliament". It is even better to face a filibuster-as some

people might call it-three or four years from now than to have us go home thinking that we might as well not come here at all. From the bottom of my heart I believe that if the minister would do as I have suggested, and if the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would accede to it, I would be up catching a 52-pound muskelunge, the same as that caught by some other gentleman about whom I read this morning. I love it up in my part of the country just as every other member likes his part of the country. I think we have been here a long time. It will not hurt anybody if the minister does what I have suggested he might do,-

On the amendment that was made after quite a large number of speeches had been heard on the terms of this bill and the threat it made to

democracy in this country, there really was nothing that I could add that would have been a contribution to that kind of a debate.
We have had many of those debates over the last 14 years that I have been in this house. One of them that I remember in 1950 lasted for some considerable time and then it was possible to make a suggestion which hon. members opposite will recall, and with which they declared that they were perfectly satisfied. I have nothing to say at this time but to make a short statement to develop what has been said already by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe). I think everybody is agreed that at this time we need a Department of Defence Production and that we need to have our scientists and our experts using their brains to devise what might be best for the defence of this country. It is all very well to talk about buying gold-plated pianos from those who make them elsewhere, but what is being considered at the present time is something far different from gold-plated pianos.
I think everyone agrees that the Department of Defence Production should be a permanent one. I think everybody agrees that there are extraordinary powers in the act and that the extraordinary circumstances of the present day make them desirable. As the hon. gentleman who has taken his seat suggested in one of his last phrases, everyone thinks that those powers, if circumstances changed, should be reviewed by parliament; and the Minister of Defence Production has said that it was his intention and the intention of his colleagues that, when circumstances justified a modification of these powers, the government would bring forth an act proposing their modification.
I want to say something that may make it a little bit more concrete and a little bit more precise, as was possible in 1950 when we were dealing with the Emergency Powers Act of that time and when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and I put our heads together to draft the things that we would put into those regulations about which the hon. member for Eglinton said he was perfectly satisfied and after which the bill went through. I do not think that the country suffered any ill consequences from the fact that the bill went through at that time. The hon. gentleman says, "Put a time limit of three years" on this legislation. I am sure he does not mean that after three years it would not be needed.

Mr. Speaker, I was glad that the Prime Minister spoke before I took the floor. I had intended to follow up what was said so well this morning by my colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), but the Prime Minister has now made a proposal which I think will allay the fears of many of the people of this country. I hope he will do me the honour of listening to what I have to say, because I do think there is a point he has

overlooked. I go along with the Prime Minister in practically every single thing he said, and I believe he will recall that when the hon. member for Acadia was speaking this morning he also went along very substantially with the position the Prime Minister has taken.
He did indicate, however, that there was some difficulty about the kind of suggestion which the Prime Minister has made. I want to point out that difficulty. I think the suggestion of the Prime Minister is better by far than the position taken by the Minister of Defence Production that the bill must be made permanent, together with all the powers contained therein; but the suggestion the Prime Minister has made is limited in its application in this house. If a private member should bring in a public bill to which first reading was given, I think the Prime Minister knows that even though he may give an undertaking at this time that the government will allow it to be discussed on government time on the motion for second reading, it may not be so discussed. It depends on who are here in the house at the time. Whether there will be a disposition to grant government time in which to discuss the motion for second reading will depend on how persuasive some of the members of the house may be at that time.
I think it would be too dangerous to leave the matter in that position. The house is master of its own rules and procedure at the time, and the house is never governed by a declaration or undertaking made by someone in times past. I think we have all experienced that, and I believe the Prime Minister will be reasonable enough to recognize that there is that very serious limitation.
There is another serious limitation. The government having brought in the bill and realizing that something should be done now that will allay possible fears in the minds of the people of the country, I think the government should bring in at this time whatever amendments or changes may be necessary to allay those fears. I make a suggestion. This morning the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) pointed out that the government already has on the statute books and is administering an act that could be used as a pattern for this act. The wheat board act is divided into two parts, and the second part of that act comes up for review every four years. In other words, the whole act is couched in such terms that it has to terminate every four years.
This does not mean it actually does terminate, but it does come into this house for review and extension every four years. As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, no one wants 50433-356
Defence Production Act the wheat board act terminated in four years. Everybody realizes that it is a good act and it does provide for the orderly marketing of Canadian grown wheat. At the same time, the powers in the act are such as to make it desirable to have the minister bring it in for review every four years, to see whether or not some change ought to be made. He must realize that; and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has brought it in regularly and has required that it be brought in regularly.
Why could that same principle not be applied to the Defence Production Act? The Prime Minister has said on several occasions, and has just now repeated, that there are certain powers in this act which should not be made continuing or permanent powers. We agree with him on that. But at the same time he is anxious to provide the minister with the very best machinery with which to provide for the adequate defence of this country. We agree with him on that 100 per cent. We want him to have an act and we want him to have sufficient powers in these very troubled times. We realize they are dangerous times, and we want the defence production minister to be equipped in every way to provide the fullest measure of defence for the people of Canada.
At the same time, as I explained when I spoke on the motion for second reading, we are only the temporary custodians of the sovereignty of the people of Canada. They have handed over or delegated it to us to use as we see best in the interests of Canada. They do not expect us to give these powers permanently to anybody, ministers or the government or anyone else. They expect us to retain and maintain the supremacy of parliament. That is the principle for which we stand now.
We can fill that requirement quite easily, I think, by dividing the present bill into two parts. Let us set up the first part of it, which declares that there shall be a permanent Department of Defence Production. Let us include in that first part all the administrative details and some of the powers. Some of these powers are not invidious, at least to us. In certain other parts of the bill there are invidious powers which I think should be separated. I am going to suggest that part II of the bill include sections 23, 24, 25, 27 and 31 of the present act. These are the most invidious. These are the ones about which apprehension exists in the minds of the people of Canada. These are the ones we would place in the second part of the bill, and then a clause could be inserted providing that part II of the bill should come before parliament every five years.

If that is done, we will give it every support. There is nothing wrong with that principle. It is much more positive than the proposals that have already been made. I think it would be reassuring to the people of the country if it were done that way, because then the bill itself would provide that every five years that part of the act should come up for review and study. If at that time parliament feels there is something which should not be there, one of these powers that is too extensive, then parliament would have the right to discuss the matter without having to depend upon the possibility of majority support for a motion by a private member. It would be possible for the members of this house to remove those invidious powers and still have the main part of the bill continue.

I think that improves the suggestion to some degree in my own mind, but I still feel that this other proposal would be better. Let me say why. In the first place, the Minister of Defence Production is most anxious about the continuing nature of the department. He wants to see that it is made permanent so he can attract to his department and keep there the best brains procurable in the country. With that I sympathize.
He wants also to be clothed with sufficient power to be able to carry forward the work he is expected to do. With that we also sympathize. The proposal I have made would give him those powers, but at the same time separate from the powers that we are prepared to grant him on a permanent basis those that may be of an invidious nature, those that may be the cause of apprehension in the minds of the people generally, and those that we have no right whatever to hand over permanently.
It seems to me that by this method we would be able to settle the matter now, rather than wait for three, four, or five years, as the case may be, upon the head of the government to bring in some proposal such as the Prime Minister has suggested. I say that the proposal I have made is better. I hope the Minister of Defence Production and the Prime Minister will give it very careful

consideration. If they do they will certainly not have any further opposition from this group. We will go along with it, and we will do everything we can to get this business cleared away.
This debate which has gone on, it seems to me almost interminably, is a ridiculous debate. It indicates stubbornness on both sides and a failure to try to come to some sort of compromise that would be in the interests of the country. The newspapers and the people across the country are talking about it now as being unreasonable. They are referring to it as a deadlock between two stubborn parties. As the hon. member for Acadia said this morning, surely we are reasonable people here. Surely we can look facts in the face and try to reach a solution that will be in the interests of the people of Canada.
It is for that reason I am making this proposal. I hope the Minister of Defence Production and the Prime Minister will indicate they are prepared to accept this suggestion of dividing the act into two parts, and making part II contain the invidious powers subject to review by this parliament every five years. If that were done, I predict that the opposition would melt away and we would get along with our business.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister a few moments ago made reference to a debate in 1950 out of which some compromise apparently was reached. That was very nice; but certainly I cannot agree with his suggested compromise at the moment.
I think we might go back, first of all, to the compromise suggested by the Minister of Defence Production on June 13, when he said:
After consulting the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to the best way to ensure effective parliamentary control over the administration of the act, I wish to announce that when the bill is in committee I will propose the addition of a third section to provide that orders made under the Defence Production Act, either by the governor in council or by the minister shall, in addition to the normal publication in the Canada Gazette, be laid upon the table of both houses of parliament at the earliest possible moment after they are made and that a notice of motion signed by ten members praying for the repeal or amendment of any such order if given within seven days of the tabling of the order in either house shall be debated at the first convenient opportunity within the next four sitting days.
Then the minister concluded:
The government has been able to think of no more effective way of ensuring prompt parliamentary control of the exercise of the powers under this act and we hope this proposal will commend itself to all sections of the house.
In my opinion this proposal does not overcome the fact that the powers are still

there, and can be acted upon forever. Once an order is issued-it might be ten or twenty years from now-the damage has been done. The damage is done before it comes to the house. That proposal is not enough.
If the Minister of Defence Production intimated that that was as far as they would go, the Prime Minister just a few moments ago offered something which in his opinion goes a step further. I must take issue with him. His offer still does not trust parliament. He intimated that the tools were required, and hoped we could see our way clear to agree with the suggestion, so we might terminate this session in a more satisfactory manner. It was intimated that the powers might not be permanent. They are; once they are there, they are permanent. No matter what kind of stand is taken on this suggestion, the thought is there that something might be done. It is on the statute books, and personally I am afraid I cannot agree with it.
The hon. member for Peace River said we must maintain the supremacy of parliament. 1 agree with that entirely. He also said, however, that thus far this debate has been ridiculous, showing stubbornness on both sides. I cannot see how arguments in favour of and fighting for the supremacy of parliament could appear ridiculous in the eyes of anyone. I think the hon. member's statement was ridiculous in that regard.
A week ago today I had the good fortune to visit the Stratford Shakespearean festival, and I think it would be a very good idea if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production were to go there and view the production of "Julius Caesar", which is now being played. In that play, as I am sure many hon. members know-a play which was written around the year 1600 by William Shakespeare-some things were said that I should like now to quote. I think they are apropos of certain sentiments expressed in this debate, particularly by the Minister of Defence Production.
As a background for what I shall say, I should like to outline what happened in that play. I do so because I think the minister's speech of last Tuesday indicated that he is thinking ambitiously, and we see such ambitions in the play written so long ago. I believe some lessons might be learned by making references to this play.
I would point out first that Pompey, Cassius and Julius Caesar formed the first triumvirate which grasped supreme power over all Rome. They divided the Roman territory into three parts, Julius Caesar having been given the northern part. In nine years he conquered all Gaul, and three times invaded and marched into Germany.

I should like to remark on what the minister said last Tuesday, June 28. An amendment was moved before the minister spoke, to this effect:
That Bill No. 256, an act to amend the Defence Production Act, be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred
[Mr. Monteith.j
to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to examine and report upon the advisability of
(a)	placing the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis and conferring on the department such powers as ought to be of a continuing nature; and
(b)	conferring for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament, such additional powers as may be strictly necessary in the light of the existing world conditions.
I think that amendment meets all the requirements that could be advanced from the government benches. Why could not the committee on banking and commerce be of assistance in this matter? The Prime Minister has suggested that there seems to be a difference of opinion which he would like to see resolved. This is one way of resolving that difference of opinion. I have noticed in the committees I have attended that the discussion is somewhat more informal, and that usually a satisfactory solution is reached. There is a meeting of minds, there is a real attempt made to actually come to a sound conclusion. A year ago this committee dealt with the Bank Act and held something like 58 or 60 meetings. They also dealt with the housing bill, and I feel they did a good job. I had the good fortune to sit on that committee. I did not contribute a great deal last year, as I was a freshman member, but I did notice that hon. members from all sides tried to reach common ground in the committee.
If this bill were referred to that committee I believe it would come up with some conclusion which might be acceptable to the government and even to the opposition. I think it would be much better to deal with this matter in that way rather than try to shove it down our throats and say, "Here it is; the powers are there forever."
As far as this first concession is concerned, I do not think there is much to it. An order might be passed immediately following prorogation and the house would not meet for another four or five months. The order would have been issued, and what good would it do to bring it up after the action had been taken?
The second concession certainly does not give parliament supremacy. This is presumed to be a concession of some kind, but I feel that the bill should be referred to the banking and commerce committee for consideration, and I am sure it would receive sincere consideration. Speaking on June 28 the minister is reported on page 5378 of Hansard as follows:
Canada's defence industry and I have worked together for the 16 years I have been responsible for the procurement of defence supplies. I have been in difficulties during that time but I have never had the slightest trouble in getting industry as a whole to come to my help in a united effort

to work out a solution. Standing here today I am very proud of the fact that in those sixteen years I have never undertaken to produce any munitions of war which I have not been able to produce and produce within a reasonable period of time.
That is quite a boast. As the hon. member tor Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) mentioned a few moments ago, in the early part of the war it seemed very difficult to achieve the procurement of munitions and supplies, and that sort of thing, but what is our situation now? In 1951, when this legislation was enacted, we were actually at war in Korea. Today I do not think there is danger of war; at any rate, there is not the danger now there was at that time. At that time we were in an actual war, but there is not even a cold war now to anything like the same degree.
As a consequence, Mr. Speaker, if this bill were passed we would be giving the minister complete power forever, or whoever might be in his place. I cannot agree with that. I do believe that the one solution, unless the bill is withdrawn and reintroduced in another form, is to refer it to the banking and commerce committee, as suggested in the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this bill, to which we have taken quite prolonged objection, is one that was presented by the minister some time ago. In his remarks on the second reading of the bill on June 7, he proceeded in an almost lighthearted way to pass it off as a thing that would be acceptable to the house, and no doubt would proceed through the house with a minimum of debate. At that time he said, as reported at page 4500 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, this is a simple bill containing only two sections. The first section provides that the salary of the minister shall be $15,000 per annum. At the present time, the salary of the minister is $10,000 per annum, but unfortunately the present minister does not draw that salary; for the moment the salary is not paid. However, occasion might demand at any time that a separate minister of defence production might be appointed-
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that this remark has been quoted before in this house. Many of us are under the impression that the statement could be taken in many ways. For one thing, as is well known, the minister holds two portfolios, trade and commerce and defence production, for one of which he says he receives no salary. What does he mean when he says that occasion might demand at any time that a separate minister of defence production be appointed? Is he perchance tiring of his amateur status in the Department of Defence Production, and does he perhaps want to load it onto one of his confreres.
If that is so, Mr. Speaker, is he trying to make the job more attractive by holding out
Defence Production Act the offer, with no time limit on the enormous powers in the act at the present time? Perhaps not. If not, then surely he must be planning to delegate some of these powers to someone else. We might well ask ourselves, to whom? To one other person? Is that person sitting in the house at the present time as an elected member, or does the minister have his eye on someone outside the house who might be available for these duties if he can be assured of continuing powers?
Power is an insidious thing, Mr. Speaker, as has been said on many occasions. It is this aspect of the problem, the continuation of those powers without restriction and without time limit, that causes us in this group the most concern.
Again on June 28, at page 5377 of Hansard, the minister referred to his association with industry, and he said this:
As far as I know it is quite happy to work under them indefinitely.

Of all the companies that have been heard since this debate started, I have heard not one single complaint from the people affected, namely, the people who are actually doing the defence production work in this country.

I can still read if I have my glasses. The point is, there are objections to this bill, and they have been pointed out by the members of this party on many occasions throughout the course of this debate. It is odd that the minister should make the claim that no one has complained, and link it up with those persons from whom he has heard while the debate has been in progress. It does lead one to wonder whether he has had some complaints, but probably not since this debate started. I might add that if industry fears to voice its protest to the government, it is small wonder, as has been explained by the hon. member for Eglinton.
One of the main arguments used by the Minister of Defence Production was that the government must be free to supervise and to expropriate. The implication in those remarks certainly left the impression that industry could not be trusted to carry on its part of a defence program. I remember an incident back in the early days of the second world war, coming as I do from an industrial city and one which is also extremely conscious of military matters. I recall the concern that was felt over the lack of armaments, and I remember that at that time the government was of the opinion that Canadian industry could not produce tanks.
I am sure the minister remembers as well as I do the fact that one of those companies in Hamilton, in an effort to prove that industry could produce tanks in Canada, actually made one, and that it rolled around the streets of Hamilton. It probably was not


the type that eventually got onto the battlefield; nevertheless it was a mute demonstration of the power and ingenuity of industry when it could produce an armoured vehicle for which it had not been tooled up in advance.
I therefore question some of the minister's statements, some of which sound very emphatic indeed. I quote him once more as reported at page 5377 of Hansard of June 28. He sought to explain away the provisions of this act by saying that after all there is nothing new about the Defence Production Act. His words were these:
It has been in force now for 16 years in this country, with the exception of a little less than a year after the munitions and supply act was repealed by this government, and I may say repealed by this government with no prompting from the Conservative party. It was repealed because it was felt that that particular act was no longer needed.
I pause there, Mr. Speaker, to remark on the different situation today. I intend to speak, in a later part of my remarks, about the statement made by the Prime Minister today; but I am amused to note that the minister claimed that this act was repealed with no prompting from the Conservative party whereas the Prime Minister is now intimating that this act which is now before us can be repealed, or at least that the government would listen to the pleadings of the Conservative party for its repeal, some three years hence. Then the minister went on to say:
Hon. members may say that the Defence Production Act is not the munitions and supply act. However, there is nothing in the Defence Production Act that was not in the munitions and supply act, although the powers granted the department in the munitions and supply act were much more extensive than those in the act now under discussion.
Mr. Speaker, I fail to comprehend how the minister can, in all seriousness, compare the conditions under which we are now working with those under which we worked in those days. In the years 1939 to 1945 we were engaged in the European conflict and later in the Asiatic one too. In 1950 we were engaged in the conflict in Korea. Powers which were asked for at that time were asked for on a temporary basis to meet an emergency which, I might say, was clearly before us. We did not need to have it drawn up for us; we needed no blueprints. We could see the need for powers of that nature. But today, in 1955, we are asked to remove from the act the clause which places a limit on those powers. Not only are we asked to do this in 1955, but we are asked to do it a full year in advance of the date on which the act would normally expire.

I have spoken about the industrialists, Mr. Speaker, and assuredly they have their problems. But it is not only industrial management which has cause to be concerned over the powers in this act. The industrial workers also have reason to be anxious. In wartime we understand that steps must be taken so that everyone literally is in the front line. Hence the workers of this country accepted the fact that their contracts were ignored or cancelled. They accepted the fact that their wages were frozen and that men were frozen in their jobs.
Even many years later this has resulted in curious situations. I met one not so long ago. A worker in an industrial plant in Hamilton went to the armouries in Hamilton to enlist. He was told that he was too old. However, he was told, "If you really want to do a wartime job, you had better go down to this other plant because they need guards and you will be, in effect, on military service if you go there and work". He did that, and he was there for about five years. In the course of the time he was there the plant for which he had worked originally rather urgently required his services and he was asked to go back. But no; he could not be released from the work in which he was engaged. He was told that he was frozen in that job.
After the war was over he eventually went back to the plant in which he had been originally engaged, and now on retirement he finds that his work was not so essential after all. He finds that the period of time he spent in what he thought was war work prevents him from qualifying for pension under the plan of the company for which he originally worked. He compares his situation with that of other workers he knows who were sent to distant parts of Canada to do war work and who, by reason of that work, were given consideration in the pension plans of the companies with which they were originally employed.
These situations are multiplied across the country, Mr. Speaker. I do not think the case I have just described is the only one by any manner of means. But there is this man who was motivated only by a desire to serve his country, who finds on retirement that he has been penalized. I think that man would do what he did all over again, even knowing that was going to happen to him, because he wanted to serve in the front line, as other members of his family and his friends were serving. But these are things we have to consider when we start to give unlimited powers for an unlimited time, without thought to whether they will be required or whether they may be misused.

What is so urgent that we need to have this matter brought up at this time? Incidentally, all the experts are not on one side of the house, despite the fact there has been a great deal of bragging going on. I was interested enough to look up the Encyclopaedia Britannica's article on governments and their classification, and I found a very interesting explanation which I should like to read to the house. It has this to say:
Perhaps the classification of most universal significance is that which is determined by the key aspect of the pattern of control: whether power is concentrated or divided. All more stable power is based in organization and the control of organization. Without common objectives there can be neither organization nor power. Power, therefore, always presupposes several human beings who are joined together in pursuing a common objective.
As I read that a vision of the cabinet appeared before my eyes. Then it goes on to quote a phrase from Aristotle's "Politics":
All human associations are established for some purpose.
Then the article continues:
That would seem to preclude a genuine division of power. Yet actually objectives that are common may be so because (1) they are spontaneously shared; (2) because they are mutually supplementary; or (3) though conflicting, they are outweighed by other considerations. If organization results in the third case, it is because those who want it get the others to co-operate by constraining or coercing them, and thus making them prefer the avoidance of the threatened penalty to whatever induced them to object.

If their objectives are conflicting, what are the other considerations which outweigh this conflict? After all, the responsibility for this act is not that of the Minister of Defence Production alone. This bill was introduced in the house by the Prime Minister, a natural enough procedure and one which is indicative of the usual cabinet solidarity. Every minister of the government is, accordingly, responsible for the bill, and I expected they would stand behind it.

I went on from there, Mr. Speaker, and looking further at the Encyclopaedia Britannica I found the description of a political party. Part of the explanation there given reads as follows:
The essential condition for the existence of political parties is freedom to form organizations that strive for power by electoral methods. Under other circumstances groups of citizens may influence the government, or they may form part of the coalition of interests supporting it; but without freedom of competition for power by electoral methods, political parties, in the strict sense of the term, cannot exist.
We are all here, Mr. Speaker, as a result of that method. We are all here because we have competed with others for the right to represent groups of citizens in this house. We are here to exercise the rights which have thus been given us as members of this house. We are here to protect the rights of all people in this nation, whether they are powerful or whether they are weak. We are here also to protect the constitution of the country and to ensure to posterity the rights for which we are merely trustees. It is not ours to give them away or dispose of them. It is ours to hand them on to all those who come after us, after having used them, in their original state.
This fear of the loss of freedom is not a new thing. For generations parliamentarians have fought any tendency to deprive parliament and, through it, the people of the nation, of any of their hard-won liberties and privileges. Many are the recorded words of public figures of other times as they fought against proposals of the day. Perhaps none was more outspoken than Edward Blake, prominent figure of the last century, one who knew the responsibilities of government as well as those of opposition. In a speech he made in the House of Commons on November 3, 1873, he had this to say:
Sir, the most dangerous doctrine to which parliament can assent is the doctrine that it should part with some portion of its ancient liberties, immunities and privileges. We ought to be most jealous with reference to each one of these. We ought to see, not merely that there does not exist some present obvious danger from the abandonment but also that there exists no possibility of future danger from their abandonment, and even if we cannot see at the moment any such danger, we must find some preponderating cause for our action before we give up one of those safeguards which have been handed down to us and which it is our duty to transmit unimpaired to posterity.
Then again, speaking at London, Ontario, in 1872, he had this to say:
Let us agree that no object can justify our parting with the least of the securities of liberty. Let us agree that there is, as all history teaches, danger, the greatest danger, in an evil precedent. I never saw a bad act of parliament passed but that it was urged, and often successfully, as a precedent for a very much worse act next session.

Such is the inevitable result. Give the precedent, and it is always stretched, and stretched in the wrong direction. A cloud no bigger than a man's hand in the morning may become by night a deluge sweeping away the very landmarks of freedom.
Those are not my words, Mr. Speaker. Those are the words of Edward Blake, spoken nearly 100 years ago. I should like to quote an excerpt from one more of his speeches given at Bowmanville, when he said:
Executive power it is which has at all times been the great foe of liberty. The name under which this power is exercised is wholly immaterial. Whether it be king, president or cabinet which wields the executive power, the constant tendency of those possessed of such power is to invade the domain of the other branches of the government and to enlarge their own jurisdiction. In the great struggle which subsisted for so many years in England out of which the liberties we now hold were gradually evolved, this was the main principle. This last was graven on the hearts of the British people and we must never for an instant forget it. I warn you to beware lest the length of time since that struggle ended should make you heedless of the prize which it secured. By gradual stages, little by little, the liberties of a people may be invaded, and results accomplished by degrees which, had they been proposed as one operation, would have been rejected as monstrous. It is then the duty of every representative of the people narrowly to watch any proposal which may tend to give larger authority to the executive than it has according to the well established principles of the constitution.
And that, Mr. Speaker, is precisely what we are doing, watching and trying in the time which is available to us to plead with this government to place upon its own legislation sufficient safeguards, sufficient limitations, that even should this government or those persons who are now in authority no longer be in this house, this country would not have powers flying fast and loose which could indeed wreck a nation that is now emerging as a major power.
We are concerned with freedom, Mr. Speaker. I hope the house will forgive me if I lapse for a moment into personal matters. It happens that I come from a family which has twice fled from persecution. Once it fled for religious freedom, and once it fled because of patriotic fervour. Those two occasions were something around 100 years apart. In the first place they fled from France at the time of the revocation of the edict of Nantes, and after finding sanctuary in Holland they eventually came to Vermont under the auspices of the good Queen Anne. There they stayed and there they were British subjects, so when the time came in 1776 that their allegiance to the British crown was challenged they fled once more to Canada.
There are many members in this house, I know, who are descended from the United Empire Loyalists. There are probably members also whose forefathers joined the refugee train from France. Today those conditions do 50433-357
Defence Production Act not exist. We have all grown up together, and we have grown to respect freedom and what it means to us. But I do wonder, Mr. Speaker, if as Blake says we have come so far from those days that we have forgotten that things can happen.
There are few public speakers who have not, at some time or other, made use of the famous words of John Philpot Curran, who in 1790 in a speech on the right of election of the lord mayor of Dublin had this to say:
The condition upon which God hath given liberty to man is eternal vigilance; which condition if he break, servitude is at once the consequence of his crime, and the punishment of his guilt.
After all, Mr. Speaker, freedom does not fall suddenly. It is a great structure which is weakened only by repeated, small but successful attacks upon its foundations. When that foundation is finally sufficiently weakened, the structure falls of itself. It is the duty of those who speak for the Canadian people, by reason of having been elected to parliament, to recognize those attacks on the basic structure of freedom and circumvent them if at all possible.
The question boils down, Mr. Speaker, to this. Are we to have parliamentary control over the departments of government, or are we to invest those departments with such powers that they need never again acknowledge the jurisdiction of parliament? If the latter is true, then we might just as well pack up and go home and leave a small group of dictators and assistant dictators here to do as they will. We do not intend to do that, because we do not believe this is a time for lip service only to the cause of freedom.
I mentioned before the remarks made by the Prime Minister. Earlier the Minister of Defence Production had issued a small but nonetheless challenging threat to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). If I took his words down correctly, he said that this will be quoted often two years hence. Well, I have no objection to being quoted at any time, and I am sure no other member of this party has. I think we are quite willing to depend upon the good sense of the people of Canada to interpret correctly the remarks we make. Threats certainly will not deter us at this time.
The Prime Minister has sought to leave the impression today that there are no threats. But many irresponsible statements have been made in the house in the course of this debate. There have been threats both veiled and naked. The Prime Minister also made reference to a concession which might be available to the official opposition or to any opposition party three years hence. Who can say who will be here three years hence?

Defence Production Act If the Prime Minister is serious about reconsideration in three years, then why not put it in the bill? If he means that, then let us have it down in black and white.
I give the Prime Minister credit for great sincerity, and this prompts me to make some comment upon a report I saw in the Globe and Mail of last Saturday on the occasion of a Dominion day dinner held in Masaryk memorial hall in Toronto, at which Dr. Alice Masaryk was speaker. In her remarks she is quoted as saying that her father had stressed the primary responsibility of each individual.

I suggest to him and to all hon. members in the house that a prayer for Canada might be appropriate also -a prayer, Mr. Speaker, for wisdom to resist unseemly and unnecessary demands for power, whether those demands be made in all innocence or whether they be the calculated campaignings of the power-hungry.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I propose to say a few words about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal, and in the course of my remarks also to deal briefly with the speech this afternoon by the Prime Minister.
IMrs. Fairclough.]
In the first place let me analyse the amendment moved on June 28. It is to the effect that the subject matter of this bill should be referred to the committee on banking and commerce for a report on the advisability of making two changes in the bill. The first of these would be as to the advisability of making the Department of Defence Production a permanent department, and giving it whatever powers the committee recommends should be of a continuing nature. The committee would also consider, second, the advisability of giving additional powers-that is, over and above those which should be of a continuing nature, and which are strictly necessary because of world conditions-but giving those powers, as the amendment says, for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament.
Obviously there is no need for the legislation this year, except to increase the salary of the Minister of Defence Production. I suggest it cannot be contradicted that this provision for an increase in the minister's salary is needed only if between now and 1956 there is to be a new minister of defence production, or if in the meantime the present minister should see fit to drop his position as Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I have been puzzled throughout this debate over how the Minister of Defence Production could place such great emphasis on the importance of his department and of its having all these terrifically wide powers, when at the same time he is administering two departments, which means that he is giving only half or less than half his time to the Department of Defence Production. Yet he tells us now that this department is of such great importance. One would think if the Department of Defence Production meant so much to the minister that he would drop his portfolio as head of the Department of Trade and Commerce and would concentrate on defence production. If he thinks that because the Russians now have the H-bomb the Department of Defence Production is of more importance, then let him drop his second portfolio. The Department of Trade and Commerce is also extremely important. The minister has not been notoriously successful in his conduct of that department, and perhaps now would be a good time for him to be like other men and content himself with the responsibilities of one department, not two.
In any event, no one is opposing the salary increase to the minister. As has been pointed out time and again, no one is opposing the making of the Department of Defence Production a permanent department of government. But surely there should be a careful study

of the powers of that department by a committee. I believe the standing committee on banking and commerce is the proper one to carry on such a study, but it might be that a special committee should be appointed for this purpose. That could be done at the next session of parliament. There would be no harm caused by the delay because the present Defence Production Act continues in existence until July 31, 1956. It has been generally admitted, even by the minister himself, that while some of these powers should be made permanent, some should not. I know the minister hates being reminded of statements he made in 1951 concerning the fact that there were these two kinds of powers contained in the Defence Production Act. However, I shall read them to him again. I am going to read them now. On March 2, 1951, as reported on page 836 of Hansard, the minister said:
There is no particular significance to this date-
He was referring to the expiry date of the act which was July 31, 1956.
-other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
In that same speech I find a further statement by the minister which we seem to have overlooked in the previous debates on the bill now before us. At page 839 of Hansard of that same day the minister is reported as having said:
Some of these powers are ones that are appropriate at any time, whether in peace, in war, or in the present state of international tension. By and large, these are the powers that are now contained in the Defence Supplies Act-
I propose to refer to that act a little further on in my speech.
-which, hon. members will notice, is only being suspended during the life of the present proposed act.
That is the fact; the Defence Supplies Act was suspended by the Defence Production Act. Here we have the minister making a clear-cut explanation that there were powers in this act which should not be continuing, when he said:
Other powers are of an extraordinary nature but fitted to the extraordinary circumstances of today.
When the minister was speaking on the resolution which preceded this bill on March 11 he said, as reported on page 1967 of Hansard:
I quite agree that all the powers set out in the act should not be continuing powers;
The minister himself has made it quite clear that some of these powers should not be of a continuing nature, but during the whole course of this debate he has declined or failed to indicate which powers should 50433-357J
Defence Production Act be continuing and which should not. The minister now wants them all made permanent, without any division between continuing and non-continuing powers. It is the duty of parliament to face this problem of deciding what powers should be continuing and what powers should not. It is the duty of parliament to insist that a thorough study be made of these particular powers, a study which can be made only by a committee in the manner recommended by the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal.
That amendment suggests, as I have pointed out, that the powers which should not be continuing should be conferred for one year only, or until extended by parliament. This has been the practice in Canada since 1939, when war broke out. The War Measures Act was proclaimed on the outbreak of war and when parliament met here a few days later the department of munitions and supply act was put on the statute books, giving the minister in charge of that department full wartime powers with regard to war supplies. It is true it was not acted upon until the following spring, as I believe the work was carried on in the meantime by what was known as the war supplies board. But we had the War Measures Act in effect at that time, and then this munitions and supply act was passed to look after the production of materials.
It is interesting to trace the course of these emergency controls. After all they were emergency controls, and they have been regarded as such right down through the intervening 16 years. The War Measures Act was put back into cold storage as soon as fighting stopped, and a bill was brought in which was a modification of the War Measures Act known as the national emergency transitional powers act. That act was replaced in 1947 by an act called the continuation of transitional powers act, 1947. Again this act had a time limit, and the government had to come back to parliament to have its powers continued. There was none of this business of the Prime Minister getting up and in a soothing voice suggesting that if any private member wanted to bring in a bill or make a motion the government would allow it to be debated. There was none of that hocus-pocus; it was written right into the statute that it would extend only to a certain time and the government would have to come back to parliament to get an extension.
What about the giving of powers to produce the supplies of war? I pointed out that the department of munitions and supply act was passed in 1939. We were right in the middle of war, but that act contained a limitation that it expire in 1943. It is true that in 1943

Defence Production Act the section containing the expiry date was repealed, but all the way through it was clearly understood by hon. members on all sides of the house from the Prime Minister of the day right down to the youngest backbencher that that was purely and simply a war measure.
I have before me Hansard for 1944 which covered a period before the fighting had ended, as a matter of fact when it was at its heaviest. At that time the government brought in a bill to set up a department known as the department of reconstruction over which the present Minister of Defence Production was to preside. He was to be No. 1 boss with power over all the other cabinet ministers in so far as reconstruction was concerned. The department of reconstruction was set up with a time limit of four or five years from the termination of hostilities. That was done because that act contained wide and unusual powers.
Here is what Mr. Mackenzie King had to say in 1944 about the department of munitions and supply act. I am quoting this because in his speech the other day the Minister of Defence Production insinuated that he had had the powers of the department of munitions and supply act ever since 1940. It is true that those powers may have been on the statute books, but they were very dead except in connection with dealing with past transactions. Mr. King is reported on page 3983 of Hansard of June 20, 1944, as saying:
For example, the department of munitions and supply was set up to carry on an important phase of war work. When the war ends that department will fade out; but, with the preparation for peace and for developing the national economy to further the pursuits of peace, it will be necessary to have some one department that will be specially charged with that all-important work. The department of reconstruction will have that particular duty.
Then in 1945 the name of that department was changed to the department of reconstruction and supply. The bill expressly placed all the powers of the department of munitions and supply under the department of reconstruction and supply. I have here a statement made by the present minister as reported at page 2435 of Hansard of November 22, 1945:
In the speech from the throne it was announced that the government planned to introduce a bill for the consideration of the house for the purpose of merging the department of munitions and supply and the department of reconstruction into a single department of reconstruction and supply.
It is worthy of notice that the time limit fixed for the department of reconstruction continued in effect for the department of reconstruction and supply. Following that, power to obtain war supplies was taken by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The

Prime Minister explained that on February 23, 1951, at page 613 of Hansard when he said:
After the close of hostilities with Germany and Japan, the powers connected with defence supply were transferred to the minister of reconstruction and supply and were carried out in co-ordination with the demobilization that was proceeding at that time. Then, still maintaining the principle of non-military procurement of the requirements of the armed services, these functions were transferred to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the responsibility for procurement rested with the Canadian Commercial Corporation, while the nucleus of a production organization was maintained through Canadian arsenals.
The department of munitions and supply was in fact dismantled in 1947. The minister himself said on June 28, at page 5377 of Hansard:
The department of munitions and supply was dismantled in 1947 and 1948 and the act became
inoperative.
In 1949 the department of reconstruction and supply was done away with. It was replaced by the department of resources and development. In 1950 the present Minister of Defence Production introduced a bill known as the Defence Supplies Act. He pointed out that it was to be the normal law for procuring defence supplies in Canada. Mind you, it contained very wide powers; it had no time limit, the explanation given being that of course it was considered as a peacetime bill. The minister was pressed quite hard during the debates; in the course of his replies he pointed that this Defence Supplies Act was a peacetime bill but that they had some war legislation all drafted to bring into effect in case there was an emergency. I quote from page 3475 of Hansard of June 12, 1950, where the minister said:
Emergency conditions would call for new legislation and for an approach to this and other questions in keeping with emergency conditions. As part of our general planning we have draft legislation in readiness for an emergency.
At page 3480 we find the following:

It is a peacetime bill.
Again on page 3490:
A purchasing bill suitable for wartime-
I repeat those words:
-suitable for wartime-
Because that is the present defence production bill.
-is in hand and that bill would be placed before parliament at that session. I am sure that parliament would enact that more drastic bill into legislation. But I repeat that what is before parliament now is a bill to govern peacetime purchases.
Later in that same year the minister brought in the wartime bill. It was known as the essential materials (defence) act and was passed in September of 1950, which of

course was after the aggression in Korea. That bill is now one-half of the defence production bill. Hon. members will notice, if they care to check, that the powers contained in that essential materials (defence) act were picked up and carried forward into the defence production department bill which was passed the following year.
It is very significant that the essential materials (defence) act contained an expiry date. There again there was no case of an undertaking by the Prime Minister to appease his senior minister; nothing like that. It was written right into the act that the act should expire on a certain day. It said that this act shall expire on the 31st day of July, 1952, and so on.
In the following year, 1951, the defence production department act was passed. As I say, it picked up the powers in the essential materials (defence) act; it also picked up all the powers that had been in the munitions and supply act; and it, too, had a time limit. We have heard many times that the time limit was a period of five years, expiring on the 31st day of July of next year. It suspended the Defence Supplies Act, so that act which is now regarded as our normal peacetime legislation for procuring defence supplies is merely in a state of suspension.
Obviously the Defence Production Act contained these two emergency sets of powers, one from the munitions and supply act and one from the essential materials (defence) act. The Defence Production Act was wartime legislation. I am not going to read this afternoon the questions and answers that came up in 1951, in the course of which the Prime Minister admitted to me that they had put into the Defence Production Act everything they could think of by way of power that would be required in wartime.

Speaking about imputations and irresponsible statements, I would point out that at page 5380 of Hansard we find this:
Therefore all the agitation we have had here is designed solely for the purpose of protecting defence contractors.
Then at page 5381:
Why are we meeting with all these efforts to protect defence contractors?
Then at page 5382:
If hon. members think that a greater purpose is served by protecting the defence manufacturers who are not asking for protection, then that is their business.
There is not a word in the minister's speech about the rights of parliament or of protecting them, because he does not understand such things.
Then what about the attitude of the minister? He said if the department was to be permanent all these powers must be made permanent. He went on to refer to the new supersonic plane and guided missiles. In his earlier speech he talked about the Russians having the H-bomb. May I say that they are going to have the H-bomb for a long time. If that is the test, then we are going to have these wartime powers on a permanent basis for a long time. The same may be said with regard to supersonic planes and guided missiles. Other and more terrible weapons will be invented all the time. There will always be new weapons of war. Then the minister talks about the mid-Canada warning line that is now being built. It is to be constructed in a great hurry, and it will be finished a long time before any expiry date set in this act would be reached. All these things are no excuse whatever for taking power away from parliament.
One needs only to refer to the minister's own departmental report in order to see that the officials of his department are perfectly satisfied with the progress that is being made with the defence production efforts of the country. In the report of Canadian Arsenals Limited we find this statement:
1954-55 was a successful year. Even should defence procurement expenditures continue their moderate decline, the company's outlook for next year is encouraging as there is a substantial backlog of orders. It is regarded as sound policy to stretch out these orders-thereby keeping our production lines in operation over a longer period and maintaining trained manpower, technical knowledge, and facilities in an effective state.
Completion of several substantial orders will necessitate reduction in personnel hired specifically for the fulfilment of these contracts.

In his speech on June 28 the minister showed clearly how he does business, and that is by making threats to industry. The Prime Minister said very naively, "Oh, you will have tabled all the orders that are issued by the minister". May I say that you cannot table a threat. Furthermore, you cannot define what goes into a threat. The minister should be issuing orders in these cases and not making threats. Neither parliament nor anybody else has any opportunity to check on these threats that are made. As reported at page 5378 of Hansard the minister said:
That right is not being used formally at the moment, but it is being used informally.
Then he referred to the defence industry now being well disciplined. Then in reporting the type of conversation he has with some of these defence industries, as reported at page 5380 of Hansard he said:
"Sorry; either you operate the plant in the way we believe will produce results or there are other ways of having it operated, for we have too much at stake here to let you decide that you do not need any help."
Is this the sort of thing that is to be permanent in Canada? The minister is now defying parliament. The other day he said that the government insists that this legislation go through. He said the government might have considered a time limit if that matter had been brought forward earlier. May I say that it was suggested by the hon. member for Peace River and myself in March when the resolution first came up for discussion. Hence that argument made by the minister is completely fallacious.
Today we have the Prime Minister coming in and saying they will not write any time limit into the bill as they did with these other bills giving emergency powers. Oh, no; they will not do that. They are going to give this minister his tools. He needs certain tools. He needs these powers to threaten people. The government say, "We are going to give him these powers; we are afraid to stand up to him; we are a spineless lot; we are afraid of this Minister of Defence Production."
