Mr. Speaker, there is an old story to the effect that when Columbus started out for America he did not know where he was going, he did not know how to get there and when he arrived he did not know where he was. As I have listened to this extended discussion, I have come to the conclusion that this story might well be related to the Liberal administration.
1 listened very carefully this afternoon to the remarks of the Prime Minister because I think we have all been hoping for some suitable compromise of the dilemma in which parliament finds itself. Unfortunately no suitable solution or compromise was forthcoming. The Prime Minister rather ridiculed the point made by opposition speakers in this debate that there is a fundamental issue at stake here. That fundamental issue is the gradual erosion of parliamentary powers that has been going on in this house as well as in other democratic bodies throughout the world. He more or less implied that the argument is academic, but I am sure there is sufficient evidence from many sources to demonstrate that there is a real difficulty facing us with respect to the preservation of our parliamentary democratic system.
It is because of this fact that the opposition is putting up the fight it is at the present time. There is some point at which a stand must be taken with respect to the gradual process of erosion, and I feel that on this particular aspect of the indefinite perpetuation of the Department of Defence Production's exceptional powers we have very excellent ground upon which to make a fundamental stand.


The debate is not entirely useless. It is serving many desirable purposes. For example, it is demonstrating quite clearly that politicians cannot be trusted too long in power. It is a rather dangerous thing when elected representatives of the people become so inflated with the sense of their own importance that they feel they are indestructible, un-defeatable and unbeatable. That was the inference I took from the Prime Minister's remarks this afternoon when he said that after another election is called and another parliament is brought together, without a doubt all the members sitting to the right of Mr. Speaker at the present time will be returned as they have been during the past 20 years.
That indicates a degree of confidence that is rather remarkable for politicians who at best have a very weak guarantee of security of tenure, and who should be under the direction of the public rather than the public being under the direction of the politicians, as has been the case to a growing extent during recent years.
Politicians cannot be trusted too long in power because of the very nature of human personality. If a human being is given too much power for too long he will quite definitely become lop-sided in his personality. He will become what is called a paranoid type, suffering from delusions of grandeur. That is inevitable, because human nature is not a fixed quantity; and if we rise to exalted levels above our fellow humans for any extended period of time it is inevitable that we will become overinflated with a sense of our own importance. The pages of history are dotted with the records of the careers of men who started out with high ideals and visionary purposes, but who as a result of the continued extensions of power became hardened and egotistical. The only solution is a change of administration from time to time. I think this debate has demonstrated that situation in no uncertain terms.
There is another encouraging reaction, too, as I see it, and that is the reaction of the public. Down through the history of parliamentary democracy the public has had a very important influence in determining what takes place by way of a legislative program in parliamentary institutions. More recently, the contact between parliamentary groups and public opinion has become more remote. That is inevitable with the increasing complexity of government today. I think the viewpoint is getting across to the public today that something significant and something basic is at stake in this issue that we have before the house. Politicians dare not ignore public opinion. They can manipulate it; they can

seduce it; they can bamboozle it, but in the long run they cannot ignore it. I think that as a result of this extended debate the real purpose behind the discussion is getting through to the public of Canada.
There is the very interesting reaction of the Canadian press, too. I wish to congratulate the members of the press gallery on the very quick manner in which they have picked out the basic issue at stake and have done their best to interpret the situation amidst the confusion and red herring appeals of the government to the people of Canada. Actually, in the condition in which our Canadian parliament finds itself today with a divided opposition, with a numerically weak opposition, the free press of Canada is the only force that stands between the people of Canada and absolutism. As I have read the editorial comments on this case that have appeared in recent weeks, 1 think the press have done an excellent job in grasping the basic issue at stake.
The history of modern political society is, in large measure, the history of ordinary, private citizens attempting to maintain control over government. I feel that this is an excellent issue upon which to make a stand at this time. I only hope that the press will not back down on the matter. The minister concerned has tremendous influence in the country, and no doubt there is the possibility that government influence generally, through the modern public relations technique, could be used to minimize the protest that is being aroused. I trust sincerely that the press of Canada will continue to interpret this issue to the public, because if the public is aroused, as it will be aroused if it knows the extent to which parliamentary powers are being delegated by this bill, then the situation is in safe hands.
I only wish that industry could protest more forcibly at this time, because as I read the Defence Production Act it is this group that is most involved in the perpetuation of the excessive powers that are contained therein.
As I read the terms of the act, the government has moved so far toward the socialist state that the balance of power between state-controlled industry and private industry has been disturbed. The state has the whip hand in these matters, and in this case the minister has the whip hand. Of course that is a very unhealthy condition for the preservation of democracy. It is this delicate balance between private and public industry that has established a sound business and industrial climate down through the years in the country south of the border as well as in our own Dominion of Canada.
Defence Production Act
The inference has been drawn in this discussion that there is some desire to protect big business in all the protest that has been raised. Back in the thirties that issue might have been justifiable, because we were faced with private monopolies of some proportions during those days. In fact I think the slogan was used that it was 50 big shots who controlled Canada.
I do not believe we are under any misapprehension as to who is controlling Canada at the present time. The cabinet has the controlling power. They have the big stick, and unfortunately those who are most concerned cannot protest as they should at this time because they would be placed in jeopardy in the struggle for orders, markets and the other things that are necessary for a profitable and worth-while business activity.
Now, coming down to the most important aspect of this debate, I am astounded that the house has brought itself into this position. My first reaction, when I began to think seriously about the implications of perpetuating indefinitely the excessive powers under the act, was one of astonishment and incredulity. The act does not expire until 1956. The fact that we have arrived at a position late in the session where we find that we are debating backward and forward across this chamber when there is no immediate urgency is beyond common sense to comprehend. Yet the opposition must continue to struggle because if it comes to a vote the result is inevitable, and the trend discernible in our parliamentary system will become a matter of statutory and legislative definition.
As I have read the various contributions of the minister and the few government spokesmen who have taken part, the picture tends to become somewhat clearer. I believe the government and the minister are somewhat out of touch with the realities of the moment. The minister, for example, in a pronouncement on the trade and general business activity of this country, is very optimistic and says things were never better, in spite of the problems faced by the grain producers at the present time. Recent statistical evidence reveals that for the first time western Canada has become displaced by the United States as the bread basket of the world. Notwithstanding the optimism on trade, there is extreme pessimism in connection with the international situation, and particularly in reference to the defence situation.
Admittedly we have been living in very perilous times since the war. I was quite impressed by the new note that appeared in the white paper on defence just a week or

Defence Production Act so ago, when, for the first time, the government were willing to admit that the prospects for thermonuclear warfare were very ominous indeed. That is not new, because I remember shortly after the war listening to discussions by those who were supposed to have the information, in which they said that it would be one world or none. As early as 1945 we were aware that we were moving into a very difficult time so far as international relationships were concerned. In Canada, however, it has taken 10 years for the government to begin to appreciate the extremities of the difficulties with which we are confronted and the minister has become very pessimistic about these matters.
Another aspect of the problem that concerns me is this. As I read through the minister's speech, delivered the other day, I thought the whole keynote of the speech was a certain suspicion of private industry. In fact it seemed a rather strong indictment of Canadian industry. The impression I got from the speech was that industry cannot be trusted, except under the long supervisory arm of the government. I suggest this would indicate that the minister has succumbed to the dominant dogma of our age, that chaos, disorder and crisis can only be resolved by increasing state control. That is the only conclusion I can draw from the remarks of the minister in the house a few days ago. For example, he makes a statement to the effect that without these overwhelming powers it is highly improbable that we will be able to meet the challenge of thermonuclear warfare in this year 1955.
Then there is another aspect of the minister's reasoning which I think is somewhat specious, so far as industry is concerned. As reported at page 5377 of Hansard for June 28, 1955, the minister indicated that there is nothing very new about the Defence Production Act, and said:
It has been in force now for 16 years in this country, with the exception of a little less than a year after the munitions and supply act was repealed by this government, and I may say repealed by this government with no prompting from the Conservative party. It was repealed because it was felt that that particular act was no longer needed.
That has no reference to the situation in which we find ourselves at the moment. True enough, absolute delegated powers were given to the government as far back as world war I in order to meet the emergency of actual wartime conditions. That same delegation of power was given again in world war II, and at the time of the Korean crisis. To claim that we need a similar absolute delegation of power today is, I submit, specious reasoning of the worst kind. We must remember that

the situation today is quite different. We must also remember that wartime conditions almost destroyed our civilization and our way of life. Certainly wartime emergencies played havoc with the preservation of the delicate balances necessary to the preservation of democracy.
Someone has said that war is the devil's playground, in that all basic institutions are weakened under the emergency crisis of war. Certainly it is true that the institutions of politics and government suffer blows from which they can scarcely recover in the postwar period.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was pointing out the difference between the circumstances prevailing on other occasions when it was necessary to resort to the over-all powers now relegated to the Defence Production Act, and I was pointing out particularly that the minister's reference to the fact that these powers had been in operation during world

war II and during the Korean emergency had no connection at all with present circumstances. There is a fundamental difference at the present time.
I should like now to move on to another specific criticism of the operation of the Defence Production Act, particularly in the years since the Korean crisis. One of the first debates I listened to in the house, on February 23, 1951, had to do with special powers under the Defence Production Act with a five-year limitation on time. On that date, as reported on page 613 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
The greatly increased defence program not only calls for greater purchases, but, what is more important, requires some direction of the production program in such fields as production, aircraft, shipbuilding, vehicles, armament and ammunition.
The present high level of demand for practically all major commodities has already made it necessary for the government to take a certain measure of direction and control or allocation of such an essential material as steel, for instance.
From this it will be seen that the government had sufficient power in its hands under the act-and a reading of the act indicates this to be so-to direct just where and how the huge expenditures of money for defence production purposes were to be made. This being so I think it is a reasonable criticism to say there has been one major oversight in the expenditure of these tremendous sums.
At the time of that debate, which is recorded on page 614 of Hansard for February 23,	1951, the hon. member for
Vancouver-Quadra asked what was to be the policy regarding the dispersal of the necessary defence production industry. There was no reply to that inquiry, but since then we have had the record of the actual operations of the department. Unfortunately that record does not present too happy a position in relation to the decentralization of the most important aspects of our defence production program, namely the aircraft industry.
There are two principal factories operating in this important area of defence production, and these factories become increasingly important with the development of the thermonuclear war threat. These two factories are located close to the two metropolitan areas of Montreal and Toronto. Whatever made the government, which was responsible for directing and controlling and developing and producing strategic air power, locate these industries in such a vulnerable position is past understanding. Today our aircraft potential could be wiped out in a very short period of time by two strategically placed hydrogen bombs. I think the government is
Defence Production Act aware of that threat, as is indicated by the alarm expressed in the white paper on defence which was tabled recently in the house.
I was not fully aware of the extent of the control exercised by the minister over such industries as the A. V. Roe company until the minister spoke just the other day. It was my privilege to visit the A. V. Roe factory a few weeks ago as a member of a parliamentary party, and I found most impressive activity going on. From 16,000 to 18,000 Canadians have been trained on the job and are doing a most creditable task in turning out the all-Canadian CF-100 jet fighter as well as the all-Canadian Orenda engine. It was a revelation to me to see what the minister said on that occasion, as reported on page 5379 of Hansard of June 28:
In the case of the Orenda engine and the CF-100 aircraft we had paid A. V. Roe company $122 million before the first finished aircraft was delivered.
I suppose that included the $8 to $9 million which was expended on the jet liner project which never came to any successful conclusion. Further on the minister made reference to the fact that there had been managerial difficulties at the factories, and he went on to say:
Consequently we took steps to strengthen the management. We called the president and managing director of the company to Canada and said, "Look here, this is not good enough. Your local management must be strengthened". He asked "where can we obtain qualified men? We started off by suggesting the co-ordinator of defence production from our own department, and he today is president of the company and a very efficient president.
Then he added this final significant sentence, which is rather strange in view of the intimation as to the irresponsibility of private industry that is implied in legislation necessitating an indefinite continuation of these emergency powers:
I may say that industry co-operated to the full, and, as I said before, I have never known Canadian industry to see the Department of Defence Production in a jam without being willing to do whatever was needed to make their contribution to solving the dilemma.
It becomes apparent that the authority responsible for this unfortunate concentration of our strategic aircraft production potential in our two largest and most vulnerable areas is this government. I should like to make that specific criticism at this time. If we ever hope to have a defence industry capable of producing the necessary air power during the difficult times, the times of dislocation that would result if war ever came to these shores again, the only solution, judging from the note of alarm raised by the defence

Defence Production Act department, is to decentralize it, to maintain the over-all operation in the various component parts.
So much for the minister, Mr. Speaker; I just want to save a few minutes for a word or two to the supporters of the government. The chief role they have played in the debate so far is that of human comptometers. They have been counting time, measuring the length of opposition speeches and generally serving in the capacity of human timekeepers. Perhaps that it why it has been possible to allow the clocks to become somewhat desynchronized during the past two weeks.
They have been waiting for the vote. Unfortunately, in a state of mind like this no amount of oratory on the part of the opposition could have any possible influence. There is complete cabinet control. But I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that lack of time is not the important thing in this debate. A good many hon. members have recollections of serving considerable time in the defence of our parliamentary system, our way of life, freedom-all the terms that are used in describing the democratic process-on the battlefields of world war I and world war II. Then time was no factor whatsoever. We were up against a military challenge to our institutions, to our civilization, to our way of life and we did not count the cost.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that spiritual erosion of our institutions is just as dangerous as a direct military assault. That is the note on which I began my remarks tonight, and I close on the same note. In considering a matter as important as this, we must always keep in mind that since world war I democracy has been on the defensive. Woodrow Wilson, who I suppose was a liberal in his thinking, summed up world war I in these terms. He said it was a war that had been fought to make the world safe for democracy. Unfortunately, just when he was uttering these words democracy went on the defensive and we had the experiences in Italy, in Germany and in Russia, with reverberations in all parts of the western world. I think Lord Grey had a better summation of the results of world war I when he said, "The lights are going out all over Europe".
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we, this parliament, the elected representatives of the people, allow this legislation, the Defence Production Act, necessary because of the continuing emergency, to be placed on the statute books with all the exceptional powers it contains, we shall be very derelict in our duty indeed.
Unfortunately in this materialistic age the forces necessary to preserve our democratic

way of life are very often neglected by even those in parliamentary circles. The quest for freedom, the desire for freedom, is essentially a spiritual quality. In this day and age of crass materialism we tend to sacrifice infinite goals for the rapture of achieving immediate finite goals.
If private industry is derelict in its duty and in its responsibilities, as implied in this act, I would suggest that no amount of regulation and control will solve the problem. The urge for freedom is the force that will decide the survival of the free nations in the long run. I would suggest very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that private members in this house should consider their actions very carefully before going all the way with the Minister of Defence Production.
There is a motto inscribed over the eastern entrance to the parliament buildings which reads:	"Where there is no vision, the
people perish." There must be enough vision -I hope there is enough vision-left among hon. members of this parliament to see exactly where we are heading in this measure. If an emergency situation arises in which it is necessary to have access to all these emergency powers contained in the act, all that is necessary on the part of the government is to invoke the War Measures Act by order in council-that is, if there is a limitation set on this measure.
We must under all circumstances keep powers precisely defined. In a parliamentary democratic institution we must avoid the acquisition of arbitrary powers; we must not make the abnormal normal. Surely we have enough faith in the cause for which we are struggling, the cause of freedom and liberty and democracy, to hope that a happier state of affairs is around the corner when we can do away with some of these emergency powers. In the meantime let us not make them indefinite; let us not put our parliamentary system in chains, because once that is done history teaches that it is very difficult to recover the ground lost.

+ + aucients had conferred such powers upon the state that the day when a tyrant took this omnipotence in hand, men no longer had any security against him, and he was legally the master of their lives and fortunes.
So much for the ancient Greek democracies. Let us now refer to the Roman republic in this regard. I wish to refer to several passages in the book entitled "The History of Government". I might suggest that if certain hon. members are a little rusty on their history, they might possibly read up on it in this book entitled "The History of Government" by Sir Charles Petrie of Oxford University. I should like to refer first of all to page 29. This paragraph well illustrates the ultimate danger of passing dictatorial powers over to one man in the face of a real or imagined emergency. I quote from page 29 as follows:
The expansion of the Roman dominions was, indeed, the chief factor in bringing the republic to an end, for the other reasons, economic and social, for the establishment of the empire were but the consequences of this expansion. Extended territorial responsibilities presented problems that the government by the senate could not solve, and so oligarchy gave place to autocracy. As so great an authority as the late Sir John Seeley said: What made the people give supreme power to Marius, and continue it to him for five years? First, the failure of the aristocratic government in 

the war with Jugurtha; afterwards, the imminent danger of the empire from the Cimbri and Teutones. What made them give extraordinary powers to Pompey, and afterwards extend and increase them? First, the alarming spread of piracy in the Mediterranean, stopping trade and threatening the capital with famine; next the necessity of exerting unusual power to crush Mithridates. What made them give extraordinary powers to Caesar? Rumours of an intended emigration of the Helvetii, raising apprehensions of a danger similar to that which Italy had experienced from the Cimbric invasion. Nothing can be more certain than the connection of cause and effect in these cases. The history of the introduction of imperialism is briefly this: government at Rome was so little centralized that the empire was unable to grapple with any really formidable enemy that assailed it either from without or within. To save themselves from destruction the Romans were compelled,-
And this, Mr. Speaker, is the important and cogent part.
-or thought themselves compelled, to resort frequently to the obvious expedient of a dictator. The more frequently they did this, the more did the republican government fall into disuse and contempt, the more did men's minds and habits adapt themselves to a military regime.
And so on. Further on in the same paragraph-I do not wish to take up the time of the house by reading unnecessary and irrelevant passages-we find this:
What wonder that in the end it supplanted the older constitution, when its advantages were so unmistakable, and the one thing it took away, liberty, was that which the populace of Rome and of Italy had never either understood or valued?
Further on in Sir Charles Petrie's book, at page 232, there is another paragraph to which I wish to refer and this is again illustrative.
I quote from page 230:
The Roman dictator held office for six months, and almost without exception his modem imitators have laid stress upon the essentially temporary nature of their functions, but all of them have been compelled by circumstances to continue in office longer than they had originally intended.

When I was interrupted I was referring to the rump parliament which, as hon. members will recall, was originally part of the long parliament. It was whittled down by the expulsion of the royalists and the Presbyterians who were opposed to Cromwell. Nevertheless, even after this Cromwell was still having quite a bit of difficulty with the rump parliament which originally was composed of his supporters.
I should like to refer to a passage in a book, though I shall not read it. I refer to a scene which should be in the minds of all hon. members, as it is one of the most famous scenes in English history. The book to

56S9
which I refer is "The Crisis of English Liberty" by Sir John Marriott. The reference is at page 306, but as Your Honour suggested I shall not read the quotation. What took place was that Cromwell who, as I say, had every good intention at the beginning, found he could not govern with parliament. He had been accustomed to autocratic powers, and parliament hampered him.
I hope this scene will never be enacted in this parliament, and I do not suppose it will. He marched into parliament one day with his army, and when Mr. Speaker was about to put the question to the house Cromwell pointed to the mace on the table and said, "Take away that bauble". Then when the Speaker objected he said, "Fetch him down".
That was an extreme case, but it was an actual occurrence in English history. People say it cannot happen here. I remind hon. members that members of the Czechoslovakian parliament said after the war, "It cannot happen here", and they left. Some of the other members of parliament said they would see their necks wrung, and it was not very long before they did.
I have some other references, Mr. Speaker, from Mrs. Spearman who was one of the recognized authorities on political science. As I say, I shall not read these quotations but will merely give hon. members the reference to the pages. Some hon. members on the other side who are so interested, or appear to be, can read them if they wish to do so. First of all, at page 169 the author points to the tendencies of modern democratic states to overflow the rule of law, which is exactly what the bill before the house is attempting to do. The book also points out how far this tendency to get away from the rule of law is removed from nineteenth century liberalism which, according to my understanding, was always the principle upon which the party opposite was based.
Then on page 174 of this book the author points out how in modern democratic states the concentration of power in the executive is continuing to destroy the democratic system. I am very sorry that I do not have the opportunity of referring to this particular passage in detail, because it sets out the matter very cogently, probably better than I can in my own words.
I should like to close my remarks by expressing the hope that hon. members on the government side and even those in the socialist party, if they cannot be awakened to the dangers to our parliamentary government in this bill by the arguments of hon. members in the Conservative party, might perhaps pay attention to some of the authors to whom I have referred. This debate is a debate on the
Defence Production Act fundamental principle of the supremacy of parliament. If parliamentary government as we know it is to survive at all, this bill must not pass.

I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment introduced by the hon. member for Royal is indicative of his very clear thinking on this matter, and indicative of the clear thinking of members on this side of the house. After all, the committees of this house are constituted with a majority of government members, so the government position on that committee could not in any way be altered from what it is in the house at the moment. If the terms of reference were sufficiently broad the committee could call as witnesses people involved in defence production, examine them, and have an informal discussion about the matter. With a lititle giving on both sides perhaps a very successful solution of the problem could be worked out.
The point in that connection is that there is no rigid control of the members in a committee as there is in the house. We do not know exactly what is the position of all

Defence Production Act government members on this particular matter, and it might be ascertained by such a reference to the banking and commerce committee. When members are speaking off the cuff in a committee they are more prone to stress their views from the heart than when they are called upon to speak during a formal debate. There may be speeches off the cuff that would not be in accordance with speeches that have not been delivered in the house. And when I say that I am referring to speeches that have not been delivered by hon. members supporting the government.
One might pose the question at this time, why the silent Liberals? It seems to me, as a very new member, that a matter of such importance as that involved in this debate would receive considerable vocal support from the government side of the house, and that it would not be left to the responsibility of one minister and two or three assistants to get up and say why the bill should be passed.
Surely the people of Canada are entitled to a full explanation; surely they are entitled to more explanation from their own members than they are receiving now. Perhaps there is more to this little struggle for power, that we have been hearing about, than is admitted. I wonder if backbenchers and others are not saying, "We will keep one foot on the ship and one on the dock. If the minister succeeds in putting this through we will say, 'Oh, we knew he was going to do it all the time, so we did not have to make speeches.' " And if he is unsuccessful in putting it through, I wonder if they will say, "Well, we knew that he could not put it through, and we could not speak in support of it." Because they are afraid if they make the wrong guess they may not get some of the plums they would like to get.
The question I pose is, why the silent Liberals? The Minister of Defence Production, referring to some of the reasons why he needed the great powers contained in this act said, as reported at page 5379 of Hansard for June 28:
I can tell you that in carrying out that same A. V. Roe development contract there were anxious moments. After we had got involved for $30 or $40 million it was quite obvious that the management of that day was not likely to produce what we required. The top management of A. V. Roe was resident in England. The man on the job just did not have the experience necessary to carry out the work, and that became obvious to all concerned.
Consequently we took steps to strengthen the management. We called the president and managing director of the company to Canada and said. "Look here, this is not good enough. Your local

management must be strengthened". He asked "Where can we obtain qualified men?" We started off by suggesting the co-ordinator of defence production from our own department, and he today is president of the company and a very efficient president. We intervened with General Motors and persuaded them to lend us their No. 2 man from the Allison engine works. He came to Canada and worked for two years on the development work. Other qualified men were obtained from industry. I may say that industry cooperated to the full, and as I said before, I have never known Canadian industry to see the Department of Defence Production in a jam without being willing to do whatever was needed to make their contribution to solving the dilemma . . . The present top man of the Orenda engine works is a man we supplied from the Department of Defence Production to take over that work. He was our director of electronics in the department. But the purpose of the act is to make sure that when we find a situation of that kind, where great sums of the taxpayers' money is at stake, we can direct the strength of the Canadian industry into the problem, and save the government's expenditure and produce the munitions which the department of defence is requiring at that time. That is the story of $122 million of public money invested in development work with the Avro company, and the Avro company today is in my opinion the equal in management strength, design strength and production strength of any aircraft facility on this continent.
Those remarks by the minister are very interesting. Was it not the glamour that attracted young Canadians to the aircraft industry? Did it not hold particular attraction to them from that standpoint? They went out and qualified themselves as aeronautical engineers, and spent hours over their drafting boards. Back-breaking hours of Canadian labour went into these aircraft. But the credit is not theirs; the credit is that of one minister. And, having taken the credit for it, there is another little nigger in the woodpile. When questions are asked about the lay-off of 3,000 men at the A. V. Roe plant, the answer is, "That is private enterprise; we have nothing to do with that."
I suggest that the answers by the government in connection with these matters should be at least consistent. Either they should accept responsibility when responsibility is theirs, or they should give credit to private enterprise when credit should be given. But the government uses the company to further its own ends, depending upon the situation at any given moment. I think a situation of that kind should be called to the attention of the Canadian people, because it shows inconsistency and the small amount of reliability that can be expected when great powers are in the hands of one man. We get contradictory answers, depending upon which answer suits the government best at the time it is given.
Under our government we recognize the value of a system of checks and balances. We have this at the municipal level. There is

no more responsible body of men and women in this country than those who govern at the municipal level. They are in immediate touch with the voters throughout the country. The municipal officers do not have great bodies of secretaries or receptionists one must pass before he can reach the inner offices. They are in day to day contact with and are immediately responsible to the wishes and individual demands of the taxpayers.
Yet at the same time the acts which create these municipal bodies say that, while being immediately responsible to the people, they have only limited powers and can only go so far. The provincial legislatures, established under the British North America Act, while holding broad powers in some fields find that the residual powers are vested in the dominion. Governments set up certain administrative tribunals, and these in turn are checked by the courts. The courts have always jealously protected the freedom of the individual. Administrative tribunals have always been kept under close surveillance by the courts when matters have been referred from one to the other. The courts have acted as a check. And the fathers of confederation said, when setting up the supreme parliament of Canada, that this house would have a form of check placed upon it, and that this check would be in the form of the Senate.
Yet despite all this we have one minister who for the time being says these great powers should be vested in him. We have a government which says that for the time being these powers should be vested in one minister, without any check or balance being placed upon him, not even the check of the cabinet. The discretion is solely in the one minister.
How foreign this is to the whole concept of our system. How foreign this is to the very fundamentals of government in any democratic country. You know, Mr. Speaker, there is a comic strip known as Li'l Abner, in which one of the characters is General Bull-moose. His slogan is that what is good for General Bullmoose is good for everybody. It is just possible that the analogy may apply. The analogy may also apply to the situation in the United States when there was a great struggle for power in connection with a great company, Montgomery-Ward. They backed up the old man until they got him re-elected, and then they threw him out. That analogy may apply here. In the face of difficulty from the outside they stand firm, but they do not honestly believe they are right, so when the time comes they will make the necessary move; they will promote him upstairs. I wonder if there is an analogy.
Defence Production Act
I also wonder what would happen under this act if some member of the cabinet, the Prime Minister included, learned through his own channels that a particular contractor was not performing a contract as it should be performed but the Minister of Defence Production for the time being did not agree that he was not performing the contract as it should be performed. What is the remedy? Does the government have the power to take over? Does this house have the power to take over? Suppose the contract involved aircraft, and it was found it was not being properly performed. I cannot see that happening with the A. Y. Roe company, which is in Peel county, but it might happen with some other company.
What would happen if the minister did not agree that the contract was not being properly handled? Would the interests with which he was dealing from day to day be approached by the cabinet, or would those interests hide behind the protection of the Minister of Defence Production? Is it any wonder that we have not heard or received too many briefs from the large interests, because they may say, "We know this man; we work with him." They may say, "This individual will give us protection; he will prevent us from being interfered with by the cabinet; he will prevent us from being interfered with by the government; he will prevent us from being interfered with by parliament; we have the one man." The interests may say, "We have him in our pocket." or he may say, "I have the interests in my pocket." But whatever the saying is, is that not a consideration?
Can we as a house of parliament responsible to the electors of this country allow one man, whoever he may be at the time, to act for us in such a way that as far as every big war contractor in the country is concerned he can be their emissary as well as ours? He can be acting in two capacities. As we know, under the law of agency that just cannot exist; you can act for only one person. Yet we would be denied absolutely the power of overriding a single minister. Speaking of single ministers, I observe that the front benches are completely empty except for the minister in question.

Defence Production Act been made, but after he spoke I was not just sure what he said. I think that is a fair statement. Someone has said this bill was his child, that it was in his name and as it was in his name he should stand up and speak in support of it. I wonder if perhaps the little child has not grown up to be somewhat obnoxious and a little bit unsavoury, and he has decided to desert it and put it on the steps of the nearest orphanage.
I did hope that when the Prime Minister spoke he would go back to what was said on the resolution stage of this bill, at which time he conferred with the Minister of Defence Production and the house leader and, as I recall, gave a rather tentative acknowledgment to the effect that consideration would be given to a time element in this bill. How simple it would have been and how well it would have been understood by all members of this house and by the country as a whole if he had risen in his place this afternoon and said, "We will make the Department of Defence Production permanent; we will make certain powers permanent, but as to those powers that we seek to put in the hands of the minister that are not in the best interests of the country for all time, which the opposition groups so vehemently oppose, we will say that they shall terminate at the end of one year, two years or three years." Then the debate would have been over.
But instead the Prime Minister suggested an undertaking. This house is not a burial place. This is a technical term, not too general but we are not undertakers and are not in the burial business. We are legislators. I suggest that undertakings of that kind are not properly presentable to the house whose duty it is to review and pass legislation, not to deal with undertakings.
Sometimes we on this side of the house feel a little like David, who went out after Goliath, whenever we oppose a government bill. After all, we are few in number and the government are many in number for the time being. After consulting the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to the best way to ensure effective parliamentary control over the administration of the act, I wish to announce that when the bill is in committee 1 will propose the addition of a third section to provide that orders made under the Defence Production Act. either by the governor in council or by the minister, shall, in addition to the normal publication in the Canada Gazette, be laid upon the table of both houses of parliament at the earliest possible moment after they are made, and that a notice of motion signed by ten members praying for the repeal or amendment of such order if given within seven days of the tabling of the order in either house shall be debated at the first convenient opportunity within the next four sitting days.
As I say, that was the first, or indirect, intervention in the debate by the Prime Minister. I take the liberty of saying that on both occasions, then and today, when the Prime Minister intervened the effect was to establish quite clearly that in the mind of the right hon. gentleman this is not a good bill, that he is uneasy and that he recognizes that there is not only some merit but in fact great logic and validity in the criticisms made against it by the opposition. On June 13 the Minister of Defence Production went on to say this:
The government has been able to think of no more effective way of ensuring prompt parliamentary control of the exercise of the powers under this act and we hope this proposal will commend itself to all sections of the house.
In so far as that proposal would give parliament some right to review orders in council and ministerial orders made under a bill which should never have been passed in the first place, of course I assume that it will be acceptable to the house; but it does not in any sense go to the root of the objection or overcome the unsound nature of the bill itself, which consists in the fact that it takes away from parliament and vests in the minister permanently, without limitation, the right to control every facet of the Canadian economy, without any reference to the House of Commons.
Then today the Prime Minister made a further attempt to sugar the pill. As I say, it was an attempt which shows clearly that he recognizes that this is not a good bill. As best I could I took down his words this afternoon, and the first thing I noticed about them was that he made an inaccurate comparison

between what is proposed by the Prime Minister today and what was done in 1950.
As I heard the Prime Minister he said something like this: "I want to say something that may make it a little more concrete and a little more precise, as was possible in 1950 when we were dealing with the Emergency Powers Act of that time and when the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Kamloops, the Minister of Justice and I put our heads together to draft the things that we would put into those regulations, about which the hon. member for Eglinton said he was perfectly satisfied and the bill went through."
Of course, Mr. Speaker, in 1950 the proposals that were made and written into the Emergency Powers Act did not give to any member of the house the right to introduce a bill to repeal the act. When we argue about these things as a matter of abstract principle, it is sometimes difficult to bring them down to earth so that the man on the street will understand, and so that we ourselves will understand exactly what is happening. So I am going to use an illustration which I hope will make it clear.
The lawyers in this house, and I think probably most of those who are not lawyers, are familiar with what we call a power of attorney. Normally, every Canadian is a free agent. He is a free citizen. He has the right to conduct his own affairs, to conduct his own business if he is a proprietor, or his own profession; to cash his own pay cheque if he works for wages; to operate his own bank account, and in every way have sole charge of the conduct of his own affairs. This freedom can only be taken away from him, without his consent, by some form of dictation or compulsion.
But it happens quite frequently, and may happen to any one of us, that an emergency arises; sickness or accident overtakes us. We recognize that for the time being we are not fully able to carry on our own affairs in our own best interests. So we approach a friend and ask him if he will, for the duration of the emergency, take over control of our affairs and administer them in our interests. Or perhaps the friend comes to us with the suggestion. This is arranged on a voluntary basis. No one is very happy about the arrangement, but it is arrived at on a voluntary basis and is the best arrangement that 50433-358
Defence Production Act can be made under the circumstances. In legal terms, the person who is overtaken by the emergency may execute a power of attorney in favour of his friend.
Then suppose, as is the case here, the time comes when the period fixed in the agreement during which the friend will exercise these powers is about to expire. The person who has given the authority says, "The time limit is about to expire and I should like to resume control of my own affairs." The agent says, "Oh, no, I do not think you are well enough yet to look after your own affairs." I suggest that right away the person concerned-perhaps I should make it clear right away that the person in this illustration is in exactly the same position as parliament is vis-a-vis the Minister of Defence Production-would get suspicious. He would say, "I gave you this authority for a limited period; why may I not have it back?" The friend would say, "I have entered into certain commitments, and I am not in a position to discharge those commitments for you until another two or three years beyond the end of the term." The person might say, "I am not very happy about it, but I will extend your authority for a reasonable period; but it must expire at the end of the time of that commitment." The agent replies, "No, I require these powers to be extended permanently and I will not consider any further time limit on the authority you have given me; I have to have complete, exclusive and unlimited control over all your affairs."
Now, sir, if any individual Canadian citizen ever found himself in that position, where a person to whom he had entrusted temporary authority demanded its continuation without limitation and without any reason being given as to why no limitation should be imposed, that Canadian would express an opinion of the man who demanded the continuation which I am not permitted to express in this House of Commons. I believe that expression would be justified by the circumstances; and that is exactly the situation which this parliament is in with relation to the Minister of Defence Production.

Now that we have that admission, I must say we sometimes wonder whether anybody took the trouble to prepare the bill and to realize its consequences. Accepting the minister's correction, I will say simply that in the course of his speech on Tuesday, he made a statement the only and inevitable consequence of which would be to lead the house and the country to the wrong conclusion. I refer to a passage in the minister's speech, where at page 5378 of Hansard he is reported as saying:
It has been said that the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom is less drastic than the act we are now discussing. I think anyone who is familiar with both acts will say that the powers in the supplies and services act are more drastic than anything contained in the act now under discussion. The defence production act of the United States is much more comprehensive and grants powers which we feel are not required in this country.

With respect to the first part of the argument, I say the minister's statement is entirely erroneous. I say that the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom is not more drastic than our Defence Production Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: You speak as an expert?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
And with respect to the defence production act of the United States, while it is true that it does go further in some respects-that is to say, it goes into fields into which our Defence Production Act does not go-it is not more drastic. Indeed it is less drastic in the sense that the defence production act of the United States is a carefully and completely drafted piece of legislation in which the powers are circumscribed and set out with detail and exactitude. Furthermore, the exercise of those powers is carefully confined within limits which incorporate a principle entirely absent from our Defence Production Act which we are now asked to make permanent. And further, in connection with both those acts-both the United Kingdom and the United States act-they have definite time limits written into them, and there has never been any attempt to take the time limit out. I have studied these acts and while, particularly, the United States act is difficult to follow-I am quite prepared to admit that it is difficult to digest, in its bulk-yet I make those statements without hesitation and without reservation.
Let me say that we feel that the way they did it in the United Kingdom and in the United States is the proper basis upon which to proceed. That is to say, if powers are to be given-emergency powers-and if they are necessary, then they should be granted, but a time limit should be written into the bill. And that time limit should not be taken out by the government without good and adequate reason being given.
Now, so far as the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom is concerned, I have said it does not go as far as our Defence Production Act. It contains a provision in section 4 which states that every order in council is to be tabled as soon as may be after it is made. It states that it is to be tabled in both houses of parliament. That is right in their act. It does not require an amendment such as the Minister of Defence Production introduced after consultation with the Prime Minister. It has been in their act since it was first enacted, in 1945. And every order in council when tabled may be annulled by resolution of either house within 40 days. It is not a mere seven days, but a resolution in either house within 40 days.

It is true that in section 6 of their supplies and services act there is an extension of the application of the powers of the minister of supply under the ministry of supply act, 1939. That is the only place where there is an extension. But the ministry of supply act of 1939 contained two very interesting and important sections. Section 6 of the ministry of supply act, 1939, provides in subsection 2:
The draft of any order in council proposed to be made under this part of this act shall not be submitted to His Majesty unless it has been approved by resolutions passed by each house of parliament.
In other words before they can make an order in council over there, under part I of their ministry of supply act, they have to have specific approval of the House of Commons to do so, before they can submit it to the king. There is no such limitation in our Defence Production Act.
Section 14 of the ministry of supply act of the United Kingdom provides:
Subject to the following provisions of this section, the foregoing provisions of this part of this act shall continue in force for a period of three years beginning with the date of the passing of this act, and shall then expire-
-provided that it may be continued by an address adopted by each house of parliament. That is the ministry of supply act, passed in the United Kingdom in July of 1939, when real world war was threatening, and was to begin within a month or so. That is the act which is extended by the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom.
But the supplies and services act of the United Kingdom itself contains a provision in section 8 which states:
Subject as hereinafter provided this act shall continue in force for the period of five years after the passing thereof and shall then expire-
-unless the two houses of parliament pray His Majesty for an order in council continuing it for a further period.
That act was passed on December 10, 1945, and was known as the supplies and services (transitional powers) act, 1945, at a time after the Labour government had come into power in Great Britain. Even the socialist government in the United Kingdom recognized they should not have permanent powers of this kind. On the contrary, they put in a five-year limitation, subject to extension from year to year. And I would point out to the house that that provision is still in their act.
I have in my hand a copy of the parliamentary debates at Westminster for November 15, 1954, which contains the report of a

Defence Production Act debate where the secretary of state for the home department moved:
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty under section eight of the Supplies and Services (Transitional Powers) Act, 1945, praying that the said act, which would otherwise expire on the tenth day of December, nineteen hundred and fifty-four, be continued in force for a further period of one year until the tenth day of December, nineteen hundred and fifty-five.
That was on November 15, 1954. That is the act in the United Kingdom; and I certainly hope the minister will not suggest that over there the defence effort is not on a scale even greater than ours. The threat to that little island from a thermonuclear bomb is incomparably greater than it would be here; the destruction would be incomparably greater than it would be from such a bomb in Canada. Yet that country, with its respect
for democracy, for the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament, finds it quite possible to do all that is necessary to obtain defence supplies and essential materials, and still keep in their act a provision that it will expire on a certain date unless renewed from year to year by parliament.
On motion of Mr. Fulton the debate was adjourned.
